# Proofs

## Presentation execution contract

**Zero LLM reasoning intervention between functions or chains is the framework's core execution claim and requirement.** LLM reasoning is confined to upstream ideation. Every runtime handoff, decision, transformation, and presentation is executed by defined functions and data.

The initial augmentations prioritize front end usability and presentation of the core deliverables, then expand into additional capabilities. P65 onward implements this sequence. The presentation runner checks registered input bytes and rejects model-client imports and network calls. New interface text uses US English; quoted source text remains verbatim.

The core rule is:

Every meaningful runtime transformation, comparison, resolution, validation, decision, and handoff must be implemented by an existing library primitive wherever a suitable primitive exists.

So when we tighten the remaining proofs, I should treat custom glue as a defect to eliminate. For example, a handwritten synonym matcher should become a library-backed lexical or ontology operation. A handwritten interval-overlap test should become an interval library primitive. A handwritten graph traversal should become NetworkX. A handwritten schema checker should become Pydantic or JSON Schema. A handwritten temporal calculation should become a temporal/calendar library. A handwritten logical implication should become Z3, Clingo, or the appropriate formal library.

These six rules bind every hardening artifact in this file and everything appended after it. They are part of this contract, not a note elsewhere in the document.

1. No hand-written implementation of an operation a library performs. Not the algorithm, not the wrapper, not the test around it. If a primitive exists, the primitive is called; if none exists, the handoff is Blocked and recorded as Blocked, never covered by local code.

2. Every primitive is researched from its own project source before use, online, at the pinned version. Not recalled from memory, and not established by an import succeeding here. The reference entry records where it was read and what was executed.

2a. When the second implementation an oracle needs is not already installed, it is searched for on the internet and installed. "No second implementation exists" is a claim that may only be written after that search, and the search is not confined to Python: another language runtime available in the environment counts, and so does a reimplementation in another ecosystem invoked as a subprocess. A candidate that wraps the library under test is not a second implementation, and its dependency list is read to establish that before it is used. Both the search and its outcome are recorded, including when the outcome is that no independent implementation was found.

3. Guard inputs are generated, not authored. Every input comes from a hypothesis strategy. An expected value is never typed by hand: it comes from a second, independent library used as an oracle, or from an invariant of the output itself, and the comparison is made by that library's own assertion callable under rule 5.

4. Zero LLM reasoning intervention at runtime. Hand-authored fixtures, hand-typed expected values and hand-written case functions are LLM reasoning intervention, and they are defects under rule 1 whatever they are wrapped in.

5. Nothing bespoke stands between the reader and the libraries. The runner is pytest. The comparison is the library's own published assertion callable, verified in that project's own documentation before use: pandas.testing.assert_frame_equal and assert_series_equal, polars.testing.assert_frame_equal, assert_series_equal and assert_series_not_equal, numpy.testing.assert_allclose and assert_array_equal, jsonschema.validate, pyshacl.validate, pydantic model_validate, z3 Solver.check. Generation is hypothesis. A guard that needs a harness, a spec format or an assertion helper that exists only in this repository is not a proof, because no reader has that file. A local `guard_runner.py` and its spec were written and removed for exactly this reason.

6. Existence is established from the library's own published source or documentation, not from an import succeeding in a virtual environment assembled here. An import proves something was installed; it does not prove the callable is public API a reader can rely on.

Compliance is not self-reported. `hardening/verify_assurance.py` counts hand-written case functions and hand-typed expected values from the AST rather than from text, checks every embedded module and evidence file against its copy in `hardening/`, checks every frozen pointer against its recorded section hash, and exits nonzero on any violation outside the frozen set.

Rules 1 and 4 were violated by every guard module embedded in this file: handoff_guards_v1 through v21 define 209 hand-written case functions and type 812 expected values by hand. The seventeen hand-written algorithms among them are replaced in the glue-elimination section; the hand-authored cases and expectations are not, and stand as recorded violations because those modules are frozen history under HG07. The correction is `hardening/test_library_defaults.py`, a plain pytest file a reader runs with `pytest` and nothing from this repository. Four hundred and thirty-three tests so far, replacing 433 of the 812; 379 remain. What those tests found is recorded in the cross-implementation register below, not here.

```
thing
-> change (functions)
-> thing
a line naming two things is a join
every function ran on the named input; every deliverable carries its sha256
```


[Open the combined workbench](proofs/out/augmentation/workbench.html). Validation details and current limits accompany each added proof.

## Cross-implementation register

Each finding below was produced by running a claim against a second, independent implementation of the same operation, with the inputs generated by hypothesis. Where the two agree, the recorded claim no longer rests on a value an LLM typed. Where they disagree, the disagreement is the finding.

The independent oracles used so far are polars against pandas, itertools against pandas, nltk's pure-Python edit distance against rapidfuzz's C++, igraph's C implementation against NetworkX, orjson's Rust serializer against the standard library, fractions.Fraction as the exact value behind every decimal rounding mode, pdfplumber on pdfminer.six against PyMuPDF on MuPDF, docx2python reading the XML directly against python-docx's object model, and python-calamine's Rust reader against openpyxl. DuckDB and SQLite are also used against each other, as are pydantic-core's Rust validator and the jsonschema package's independent implementation of the specification, checking one constraint that pydantic itself emits as a JSON Schema; portion against pandas.Interval for overlap; libxml2 through lxml against the pure-Python ElementTree for XML; and igraph's acyclicity test against NetworkX's topological order. Three of these pairs do not fully agree, and each disagreement is asserted rather than normalized away. pdfplumber collapses a run of spaces that PyMuPDF preserves and omits the trailing newline PyMuPDF adds, so a claim of literally recovered PDF characters depends on which extractor ran. DuckDB evaluates 7/2 as 3.5 where SQLite truncates to 3, so a cost or allocation query written against one engine does not carry to the other. DuckDB sorts nulls last and SQLite sorts them first, so the smallest or earliest row selected by an ORDER BY with LIMIT is engine-dependent. The two engines do agree that an aggregate over an empty selection is null rather than zero, which independently confirms the finding recorded for P143 and P147. A fourth disagreement is larger than any of these. workalendar, an independent implementation of working-day arithmetic, and numpy.busday_offset return different dates whenever the anchor is not a working day: workalendar counts the next working day as the first one added, while numpy rolls the anchor forward and then adds, so the results differ by exactly one working day. Over every day of 2026 and offsets of one, two and five, the two agreed on all 783 working-day anchors and differed on all 312 non-working anchors, with no exceptions. They agree on which days are working days, so the divergence is about counting rather than about the calendar. Any chain that offsets from a date which may not be a working day gets a different answer depending on which library computed it, which reaches the due dates of P173, whose anchors include a planned start, and the offsets recorded for P142 and P182. What each project documents was then read at the pinned versions, which the earlier entry had not done. numpy 2.4.6 documents the convention in the first sentence of busday_offset, at raw.githubusercontent.com/numpy/numpy/v2.4.6/numpy/_core/multiarray.py: "First adjusts the date to fall on a valid day according to the ``roll`` rule, then applies offsets to the given dates counted in valid days." It documents the default as roll='raise', which "means to raise an exception for an invalid day", and its own examples name both readings of the question, labelling roll='forward' with offset 0 "First business day on or after a date" and roll='backward' with offset 1 "First business day after a date". workalendar 17.0.0 documents nothing of the kind: add_working_days, at raw.githubusercontent.com/workalendar/workalendar/17.0.0/workalendar/core.py, says only "Add `delta` working days to the date", and its loop steps one calendar day at a time from the anchor and increments the count only when is_working_day accepts the day, so the anchor is never examined and never counted. Executed, that turns out not to be a third convention but one of numpy's own: over every day of 2026 and every offset from one to twenty, workalendar's result equals numpy's under roll='backward' in all 7300 pairs, and for negative offsets of the same sizes it equals numpy's under roll='forward' in all 7300. workalendar rolls the anchor away from the direction of travel, so no single roll rule matches it in both directions and a chain cannot pick one and be right about both. The divergence is therefore between two documented options of one library rather than between two calendars, and the 'forward' the chains pass is a choice someone made: the documented default refuses a non-working anchor with a ValueError instead of answering. Two further divergences follow from the same method. The standard library's zoneinfo and dateutil.tz agree on every generated timestamp away from a transition and disagree inside a nonexistent local time: for 2026-03-08 02:xx in America/New_York, where the clock jumps from 02:00 to 03:00, zoneinfo resolves the gap with the pre-transition offset and dateutil with the post-transition one, and neither raises. And arrow returns a naive timestamp as UTC where datetime.fromisoformat returns it naive, so a chain that validates UTC timestamps by parsing them gets a different answer depending on which parser ran; this is the second implementation behind the P156 finding that fromisoformat is a parser rather than a validator. A claim recorded here earlier, that no second implementation was available to check dateutil's RRULE expansion, was written without a search and is withdrawn under rule 2a. The search found that every Python candidate delegates to dateutil: recurring-ical-events declares python-dateutil as a dependency and its rrule module imports rrule, rruleset and rrulestr from it, and iCal-library documents that it relies on dateutil for RRule support, so neither is a second implementation. rrule.js and rrule-go are documented ports of the dateutil module and inherit its behaviour by construction. php-rrule was then cloned and read. Its README states, verbatim, "This library started as a port of python-dateutil", so it is a separately maintained port in another language and runtime, not an independent implementation, and rule 2a's search records it as such. Run under PHP 8.4.19 as a subprocess oracle, it agrees with dateutil on every generated case: identical occurrences on days 1 to 28 for every count, the same seven omitted short months from a day-31 anchor, and the same month ends under BYMONTHDAY=-1. That agreement establishes the behaviour in two runtimes; it does not by itself establish what the standard requires, since a port inherits the design it was ported from. The standard was then read. Three hosts carrying RFC 5545 are blocked from this environment, but dateutil's own installed source quotes section 3.3.10 in a docstring, verbatim: "Recurrence rules may generate recurrence instances with an invalid date (e.g., February 30) or nonexistent local time (e.g., 1:30 AM on a day where the local time is moved forward by an hour at 1:00 AM). Such recurrence instances MUST be ignored and MUST NOT be counted as part of the recurrence set." The month-skipping recorded for P182 is therefore what RFC 5545 mandates, not a library quirk: a MONTHLY rule anchored on the 31st is required by the standard to produce no occurrence in a month without a 31st, and any implementation that instead clamps to the month end is the nonconforming one. The P182 finding stands, reclassified from a library-default gap to a specification behaviour the chain must state. The largest disagreement found so far is in CSV reading, where four independent readers give three answers to the same bytes. For a row whose second field is a quoted empty string and whose third is an unquoted empty field, the standard library's csv module returns two empty strings, pandas returns two missing values, pyarrow returns two empty strings, and polars alone keeps the two apart. Worse, a field whose literal text is one of null, NULL, NA, N/A, NaN, nan, None, n/a or 1.#IND is returned as text by the standard library and by polars and is turned into a missing value by pandas even when the column is read with dtype=str, and by pyarrow for all of those but None. The two coercing readers therefore do not agree with each other on their own sentinel sets. A column whose real content is NA, the ISO code for Namibia, survives in two readers and is destroyed in the other two, silently and with no option passed. This reaches P137, whose recorded claim that quoted empty strings remain distinct from nulls holds in exactly one of the four readers, and every chain that reads a CSV, including P152 and P168. The two workbook readers the chains pair on every native-table claim disagree in the same way. A cell written as a formatted date reads as a datetime.datetime from openpyxl and as a datetime.date from python-calamine, and those two are not equal in Python. An integer cell reads as int from one and float from the other. A formula cell reads three ways: openpyxl returns the formula text by default, returns the cached value when opened with data_only=True, and calamine returns that cached value as a float, so the default openpyxl read is the one that is not a number at all. Dozens of chains record that both workbook readers agree on a stated number of cells. They agree only after a type normalisation that none of them states, and on a workbook containing formulas they agree only if openpyxl was opened with data_only=True. Canonical JSON is the same story. The chains seal manifests with json.dumps(sort_keys=True) and a sha256; P262 names RFC 8785 as the canonicalisation standard. The two agree on integer objects inside the shared domain and differ otherwise: RFC 8785 writes a float with no fractional part as an integer literal where json.dumps keeps the trailing .0, erases the sign of negative zero where json.dumps preserves it, and refuses any integer outside plus or minus 2**53 - 1, a symmetric exclusive bound, where json.dumps serialises arbitrary precision. A seal computed one way therefore does not match a seal computed the other, and the standard one has the smaller domain. The three serializers exercised here have three different integer domains: unbounded for the standard library, asymmetric from -2**63 to 2**64 - 1 for orjson, and plus or minus 2**53 - 1 for RFC 8785. A fourth difference is more consequential than the value formatting, because key order is the substance of canonicalisation: RFC 8785 sorts keys by UTF-16 code unit as the standard requires, while json.dumps(sort_keys=True) sorts by code point. A supplementary-plane character encodes as a surrogate pair beginning at D800, which is below E000, so for keys spanning the plane boundary the two orders are opposite. Hypothesis found that case rather than an author choosing it. Two independent Markdown renderers were also compared. markdown-it-py and Python-Markdown agree on headings, lists, emphasis, hard breaks, raw HTML and on escaping an ampersand and a less-than, which corroborates the escaping claims recorded for P105 and P114; they disagree on a line following an empty blockquote marker, which Hypothesis found in three characters. markdown-it-py closes the quotation and places the line outside it while Python-Markdown treats it as a lazy continuation and places it inside, so a quoted passage becomes unquoted, or the reverse, depending on which renderer ran. P195's own subject was examined the same way, with the regex module's UAX#29 grapheme clustering as the implementation independent of unicodedata's normalisation. P195's contract tags every offset as bytes or Unicode code points. There is a third space it does not name: a Devanagari consonant with its vowel sign, and an emoji with a skin-tone modifier, are each one grapheme and two code points, and NFC leaves both at two, so normalisation never closes the gap and a span expressed in code points can split a cluster. The normalisation form is load-bearing in a second way. NFC leaves the fi ligature, Roman numeral twelve, one half and a circled digit untouched, while NFKC replaces all four: the first three become longer, so every later offset moves, and the circled digit becomes a plain digit of the same length, so an offset map built before normalisation still validates afterwards while the character underneath it has been substituted. A span map checked only by length cannot detect that case at all.

The financial primitives of P178 and P179 were then run against a second implementation in another language. numpy-financial 1.0.0 is pinned by the chains; the oracle is pyxirr 0.10.8, a Rust extension built with maturin. Its pyproject.toml at the v0.10.8 tag (raw.githubusercontent.com/Anexen/pyxirr/v0.10.8/pyproject.toml) declares no [project] dependencies, and its Cargo.toml at the same tag lists only pyo3, the rust-numpy bindings, time and ndarray, so rule 2a's check that a candidate does not wrap the library under test is satisfied from its own dependency list. Both libraries were read at their pinned versions before use: numpy-financial's _financial.py at raw.githubusercontent.com/numpy/numpy-financial/v1.0.0/numpy_financial/_financial.py, pyxirr's periodic functions at raw.githubusercontent.com/Anexen/pyxirr/v0.10.8/src/core/periodic.rs and its Python signatures at .../v0.10.8/docs/functions.md. They agree on more than the proofs claimed. The periodic payment agrees to nine significant figures over generated rates from zero to a half, terms to sixty periods and principals to a million, including the zero-rate branch each library special-cases separately, and both sign it as cash out: numpy-financial's pmt docstring carries the equation "fv + pv*(1 + rate)**nper + pmt*(1 + rate*when)/rate*((1 + rate)**nper - 1) == 0" and pyxirr documents "By convention, investments or 'deposits' are negative, income or 'withdrawals' are positive." Net present value agrees to nine figures on generated flows, and pyxirr's documented alternative convention, "By default, npv function starts from zero (numpy compatible), but you can call it with start_from_zero=False parameter to make it Excel compatible", is exactly one period of discounting from the numpy convention, which replaces P179's typed ratio of 1.08 with an invariant of the two outputs. The internal rate agrees to six figures for flows that change sign once, even though the solvers share no method: numpy-financial takes the roots of the cash-flow polynomial with np.roots and keeps the root nearest zero, while pyxirr runs Newton-Raphson and falls back to Brent's method. Three divergences remain, and each one lands on something P178 or P179 recorded as a fact about the operation rather than about the library. First, the interest portion outside the loan term. numpy-financial 1.0.0 computes ipmt as _rbl(rate, per, total_pmt, pv, when)*rate with no range check on per at all, so a period before the loan starts or after it ends returns a finite number; pyxirr's Rust core returns f64::NAN there under the comment "payments before first period don't make any sense." and its float_or_none converts that NaN to None. P178's recorded observation that a period past the term "returns a number" is therefore a numpy-financial default rather than a property of amortisation, and an off-by-one loop over a schedule is silently wrong in one library and visibly empty in the other. Second, a conditioning divergence inside the term that no proof anticipated. The two libraries compute the same interest portion by algebraically equivalent but numerically different routes, numpy-financial through its future-value formula and pyxirr through one simplified closed form, and the gap grows with (1 + rate)**nper: below 1e-10 relative for every term to sixty periods at rates to a fifth, and 1.6e-5 relative in the final period of a sixty-period term at rate 0.5. Nothing raises and neither value is nan, so an amortisation schedule reconciled to the cent against the other library does not balance, and the agreement recorded for P178 holds in a region with a boundary rather than everywhere. Third, the two libraries partition the failures of the internal rate differently, and neither partition refines the other. numpy-financial folds cash flows that never change sign, all-zero flows and a failed root search into the same nan, and raises numpy.linalg.LinAlgError when a flow is missing; pyxirr raises InvalidPaymentsError for the ill-posed sign case, documented as "negative and positive payments are required", reserves None for a failed search, and returns None rather than nan when a flow is missing, from npv as well as from irr. P179's title, that one nan carries three different reasons, is confirmed for numpy-financial and is a property of that library alone: the second implementation keeps two of the three apart, and moves the missing-flow case from an exception to a silent None. A chain that tests for nan to detect an unanswerable cash-flow question detects nothing under pyxirr, and a chain that catches LinAlgError to detect a missing flow catches nothing there either.

P183 and P185 both move a date a whole number of months from an anchor that is the end of a month, and both record the result as a fact about the calendar. Two other runtimes say otherwise. Ruby 3.3.6's Date#>> is a C implementation in that language's standard library with no relation to dateutil, read at tag v3_3_6 in raw.githubusercontent.com/ruby/ruby/v3_3_6/ext/date/date_core.c, where the documentation states, verbatim, "When the same day does not exist for the new month, the last day of that month is used instead", and d_lite_rshift decrements the day until valid_civil_p accepts it. PHP 8.4.19's DateTime::modify is C over timelib; its manual was read in a clone of php/doc-en at commit d8de774ae203bccf3ffe02895d8c8fc754377451, where reference/datetime/datetime/modify.xml carries an example headed "Beware when adding or subtracting months" whose stated output is 2001-01-31 followed by 2001-03-03, and reference/datetime/formats.xml documents day overflow as "Day 0 means the last day of previous month, whereas overflows count into the next month." dateutil 2.9.0.post0 was read at its own tag, raw.githubusercontent.com/dateutil/dateutil/2.9.0.post0/src/dateutil/relativedelta.py, where __add__ computes day = min(calendar.monthrange(year, month)[1], self.day or other.day). Run over month ends generated from 1901 to 2199 and offsets from minus sixty to sixty months, through shims that only parse argv, call the library and print, dateutil and Ruby agree on every case. PHP was compared over the month ends of the months the calendar module reports as having thirty-one days, at offsets of one to sixty months, with the two regions separated by dateutil's own output rather than by any rule written here, so that no generated input is discarded. It agrees on every case in which the anchor day exists in the target month and differs on every case in which it does not, with no exception in either direction, and its answer is always the later one, because it counts the missing days forward into the month after instead of stopping at the month end. Nothing raises. A term or an expiry computed in PHP is therefore one to three days later than the same term computed in Python, and only for anchors at the end of a long month, which is exactly the anchor P183 and P185 use. A third implementation agrees with dateutil and is corroboration rather than independent confirmation: shift_month in raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/v2.2.3/pandas/_libs/tslibs/offsets.pyx computes day = min(stamp.day, days_in_month), and its own docstring says the day is "determined by day_opt using relativedelta semantics" and describes the default as "the same day as the input, or the last day of the month if the new month is too short". Two of the three implementations a chain is likely to reach share the convention by declaration; the third runtime does not share it at all. The repair is not to prefer a library. PHP has a phrase for the operation the chains actually mean, documented as setting "the day to the last day of the current month", and asked that question rather than for a month offset it agrees with dateutil's relativedelta(months=+1, day=31) on every generated month end. So P183's anniversary and P185's renewal term have to name which of the two operations they are, an offset that clamps or a month end, because the anchor they use is the one place where those two operations differ.

P196 builds a closure over a reference graph and resolves each reference against a base, and both halves were run against implementations that share no code with the ones the proof names. On the graph half, networkx 3.6.1 and python-igraph 1.0.0 agree on every generated reference graph about the strongly connected components, which is the cycle test P196 runs separately, and they agree about reachability once one convention is matched. That convention is the finding. Both projects describe the operation in one line and describe it the same way: python-igraph documents subcomponent with mode="out" as returning "the vertex IDs which are reachable from the given vertex" (raw.githubusercontent.com/igraph/python-igraph/1.0.0/src/_igraph/graphobject.c) and networkx documents descendants as "Returns all nodes reachable from `source` in `G`" (raw.githubusercontent.com/networkx/networkx/networkx-3.6.1/networkx/algorithms/dag.py). They differ by the root. On a ring, and on a single self-loop, the root really is reachable from itself; igraph returns it and networkx does not, because descendants is implemented as the children of bfs_edges and its own docstring adds, two lines under that summary, that "The `source` node is not a descendant of itself, but can be included manually". A closure taken from a node that participates in a reference cycle is therefore one short, which is exactly the graph P196 is about. On the resolution half, rule 2a's search found two independent implementations rather than none. rfc3986 2.0.0 implements RFC 3986 section 5 in its own code, and its setup.cfg at tag 2.0.0 declares no install_requires at all (raw.githubusercontent.com/python-hyper/rfc3986/2.0.0/setup.cfg), so it does not wrap urllib; node v22.22.2's URL implements the WHATWG URL Standard, a different specification from the RFC the standard library follows, which is itself worth stating because the chains say only that a reference is resolved. The three agree on every generated ordinary reference: relative segments, dot segments, a fragment. They diverge three times, and each divergence changes the string a chain would store as a document's identity. urljoin alone keeps the case of the host, where rfc3986 normalises it and the WHATWG parser lowercases it, so one resolver produces two unequal strings for one resource and a closure that deduplicates by string keeps both. urljoin alone leaves a space in the reference unencoded, where the other two write %20. And a reference beginning with a backslash resolves three different ways: urljoin keeps it as an ordinary path character under the base directory, rfc3986 percent-encodes it as %5C under the same directory, and the WHATWG parser reads it as a path separator, making the reference absolute from the root, so that one of the three fetches a different document altogether. This is the CSV situation in another place: the readers do not agree with each other about what the same bytes mean, and the disagreement is silent.

P193 reports what an unsatisfiable core does and does not name, and P197 reports that two reasoning engines answer a missing count differently. Both were re-run against a second solver. Rule 2a's search for an implementation independent of z3 found cvc5, whose wheel at version 1.3.4 declares no Python dependencies and imports nothing from z3; its pythonic layer imitates z3's API deliberately, which is worth stating, but the decision procedure underneath is cvc5's own C++. Both projects' descriptions of the core were read at the pinned versions: z3 5.1.0 documents unsat_core as returning "a subset (as an AST vector) of the assumptions provided to the last check()" (raw.githubusercontent.com/Z3Prover/z3/z3-5.1.0/src/api/python/z3/z3.py), and cvc5 1.3.4's own header says of getUnsatCore that after a check with assumptions "A subset of those assumptions may be included in the unsatisfiable core returned by this function." (raw.githubusercontent.com/cvc5/cvc5/cvc5-1.3.4/include/cvc5/cvc5.h). Neither promises a minimum and neither promises uniqueness, and the executed result shows why that matters. On generated sets of integer bounds the two solvers return the same status every time, and each solver's core, replayed as the whole problem in the other solver, is still unsatisfiable, so a core really is a sufficient subset. But given four bounds in which two separately contradict a third, the two solvers return different cores for every one of a thousand generated anchors, never the same one, both strict subsets and both valid. P193's finding is therefore not a fact about z3's core; it is a fact about cores. A rule absent from the core is not thereby consistent, and a conflict report built from one solver's core does not reproduce on another solver, which is a stronger obligation than the proof records. P197 came out the other way. clingo 5.8.2, whose README describes it as computing answer sets for Answer Set Programming, and z3 agree on every generated count and threshold while the count is present: the atom is derived exactly when the constraint is satisfied. Remove the fact and they part in the direction that matters. z3 finds both the threshold and its negation satisfiable, so the question is open; clingo derives nothing, so the approval is absent from the answer set. A caller reading "not approved" out of the answer-set engine cannot tell a refusal from a missing record, and a caller reading satisfiability out of the SMT engine cannot tell an approval from a possibility. That is the closed-world assumption rather than a defect in either engine, and it is a handoff obligation the chain has to state.

P186 reports that one default flag decides which progress figure a cutoff sees, and that the primitive refuses unsorted input. The second implementation is polars 1.44.1's join_asof, Rust against the Cython and numpy of pandas 2.2.3's merge_asof. On sorted event tables the two agree on every generated cutoff, including a cutoff before every event, where both return a missing value and neither returns zero. Both engines expose the flag, spelled allow_exact_matches in each, and both move the answer by one row when the cutoff falls exactly on an event, so P186's two reported percentages are a flag rather than a fact and the agreement is now across engines. The refusal is not. pandas raises ValueError with the message that right keys must be sorted. polars raises InvalidOperationError for the same unsorted frame when the join has no by column, and when a by column is present it cannot check at all: it warns, verbatim, "Sortedness of columns cannot be checked when 'by' groups provided", and returns an answer. The answer is wrong in the direction that hides work. polars scans the right frame in the order it is given and stops at the first key past the cutoff, so moving the last event to the front makes the join report no update at all where the sorted frame reports one, and a warning is the only sign. Over one small table the four orderings of four events produced four different answers, one of them a missing value, and none of them raised. P186's recorded claim that the primitive refuses unsorted keys therefore holds for pandas and fails for polars in exactly the shape the chain uses, since it is the by-group join, grouping by task, that loses the check.

P184 turns on a unit library refusing an operation. The second implementation is unyt 3.1.0, whose pyproject.toml at tag v3.1.0 (raw.githubusercontent.com/yt-project/unyt/v3.1.0/pyproject.toml) lists numpy, sympy and packaging and does not depend on pint. It has both the absolute and the delta temperature units, and it agrees with pint 0.25.3 on every generated reading: the same Fahrenheit-to-Celsius conversion, the same span conversion, the same psi-to-kilopascal conversion, and the same constant gap between converting a span as a span and converting it as a temperature, a gap that does not depend on the reading, which is why the mistake P184 records survives review. It looks like a plausible number. The refusal does not carry. pint's documentation at 0.25.3 (raw.githubusercontent.com/hgrecco/pint/0.25.3/docs/user/nonmult.rst) states the reason: "the addition of quantities with offset units is ambiguous, e.g. for *10 degC + 100 degC* two different result are reasonable depending on the context, *110 degC* or *383.15 degC (= 283.15 K + 373.15 K)*. Because of this ambiguity pint raises an error for the addition of two quantities with offset units (since pint-0.6)." unyt performs the addition and returns the first of those two readings, for every generated pair, with no warning and no error. The guard P184 leans on is therefore one library's policy rather than a property of the dimension, and a chain that changes unit library loses the check that a temperature and a temperature cannot be summed. The dimensional guard does carry: both libraries refuse to convert a temperature to a pressure, though they raise different exception types, so code that catches pint's DimensionalityError catches nothing under unyt.

P157 builds a depreciation schedule, generating its periods with pandas.period_range and recomputing its month ends with dateutil.relativedelta, and case 157 of handoff_guards_v16 records as a discovery that walking the schedule one month at a time and offsetting each instalment from the acquisition date give different answers. Two other runtimes document that difference in their own manuals. Ruby 3.3.6's Date#>> is C in that language's standard library; its docstring at tag v3_3_6 (raw.githubusercontent.com/ruby/ruby/v3_3_6/ext/date/date_core.c) introduces the case with the words "This results in the following, possibly unexpected, behaviors:" and then shows both halves of case 157, "d1 = d0 >> 1 # => #<Date: 2001-02-28>" followed by "d2 = d1 >> 1 # => #<Date: 2001-03-28>" for the schedule walked a month at a time, and "d2 = d1 >> -1 # => #<Date: 2001-01-28>" for the offset that does not come back. PHP 8.4.19's DateTime::modify carries the same warning from the other side: the manual source in the clone of github.com/php/doc-en at commit d8de774ae203bccf3ffe02895d8c8fc754377451 (reference/datetime/datetime/modify.xml) heads an example "Beware when adding or subtracting months" and prints 2001-01-31 and then 2001-03-03 for two successive modify('+1 month') calls on 2000-12-31. dateutil 2.9.0.post0 documents the clamp itself, in docs/relativedelta.rst at that tag (raw.githubusercontent.com/dateutil/dateutil/2.9.0.post0/docs/relativedelta.rst), where it says "If the result falls on a day after the last one of the month, the last day of the month is used instead" and its doctest shows date(2003,1,31)+relativedelta(months=+2) returning 2003-03-31; it says nothing about what changes when the same offset is applied in stages, and the implementation is the single line day = min(calendar.monthrange(year, month)[1], self.day or other.day) in src/dateutil/relativedelta.py at that tag. Executed rather than quoted, the three implementations divide as follows. Over the whole region where dateutil's two hops differ from its single offset, Ruby's two hops differ from Ruby's single offset by exactly the same date, and always earlier; pandas 2.2.3's DateOffset agrees with dateutil on every generated split and every generated reversal, needing no region at all. PHP diverges: on that same region its two hops land strictly later than its own single offset, every time, so a chain that computes an instalment schedule in one runtime and an anniversary schedule in the other does not merely carry the drift, it carries it with the opposite sign. The reversal is sharper still. The set of offsets that do not return to the anchor is the same set in both conventions, every offset where dateutil fails to come back being an offset where PHP fails to come back, and the two miss the anchor on opposite sides, dateutil and Ruby landing before it and PHP after it, while on the complementary region all three return. The other half of the case asks pandas for the end of a period: Period.end_time falls on the day PHP calls "last day of this month" for every generated month, but the value returned is the last representable nanosecond of that day, so a cutoff written as period_end == Timestamp(day) is false for every month. What this changes in P157 is that the choice between stepping and offsetting is not an implementation detail the chain may leave to whichever primitive is at hand: it is a documented fork in three separate calendars, and the sign of the error follows the runtime.

P159 scores a risk register, bands each score with pandas.cut and counts the pairs with numpy.histogram2d, and case 159 of handoff_guards_v16 records that rows outside the declared scale vanish from the matrix without an error. The second implementation is polars 1.44.1, Rust, whose py-polars/pyproject.toml at tag py-1.44.1 (raw.githubusercontent.com/pola-rs/polars/py-1.44.1/py-polars/pyproject.toml) declares exactly one dependency, polars-runtime-32, and nothing from pandas or numpy. The two projects mean different things by the list of numbers they are handed, and each says so in its own source. pandas' docstring at v2.2.3 (raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/v2.2.3/pandas/core/reshape/tile.py) describes the argument as "sequence of scalars : Defines the bin edges allowing for non-uniform width. No extension of the range of `x` is done"; polars' docstring at the tag (py-polars/src/polars/series/series.py, a path that moved under py-polars/src at this version) describes its argument as a "List of unique cut points" and its own example turns two cut points into three categories, the first of them (-inf, -1]. So pandas bins the interval between the outermost numbers and polars bins the whole line. Executed on generated edges and generated scores, the two agree on the band of every score strictly inside the scale, under both closures. Outside it they part completely: every score at or below the lowest edge is null in pandas and, in polars, sits in an unbounded band whose endpoint is that edge, and under the left-closed reading the same thing happens at the top with a band running to positive infinity. The rows P159 records as dropped are, in the other engine, silently kept in a band with no floor, which is the more dangerous of the two behaviours because nothing downstream can tell that band from a measured one. The chain's own two primitives also disagree with each other: numpy.histogram counts a score sitting exactly on the lowest declared edge, because its first bin is closed on the left, while pandas' default right-closed cut returns null for it, and turning the closure round moves the loss to the highest declared score rather than removing it. pandas' remedy for the low end moves the boundary instead of closing the interval: its source defines adjust = lambda x: x - 10 ** (-precision) and applies it under the comment "adjust lhs of first interval by precision to account for being right closed", so with include_lowest the first band pandas reports starts strictly below the edge that was declared, and the score then lands in the first declared band while polars still reports it below all of them. On the counting half, with every pair inside the scale the histogram total equals the number of rows and so does the polars group-by count, but numpy returns the cell counts as floating point where the polars aggregation returns unsigned integers; with some pairs above the scale the histogram total falls to the number of in-scale rows while polars still counts every row. What this changes in P159 is that neither the count of assessments nor the band an assessment falls in survives a change of engine, and the two primitives the proof already uses together do not share a convention at the endpoints.

P155 loads a journal with beancount 3.2.3 and case 155 of handoff_guards_v16 records that a balance assertion one cent wrong passes while the same figure written with one more decimal digit is rejected. Rule 2a's search for a second implementation of the Beancount file format found four candidates and one usable one. beancount-parser-lima, Rust, is installed here as a wheel at 0.6.0 and imported directly; its README at tag 0.6.0 (raw.githubusercontent.com/tesujimath/beancount-parser-lima/0.6.0/beancount-parser-lima/README.md) calls it "A zero-copy parser for Beancount in Rust" that "is intended to be a complete implementation of the Beancount file format, except for those parts which are deprecated", and its Cargo.toml at the same tag lists chumsky, logos, rust_decimal, time and pyo3 and nothing from the Python package, which is what makes it independent. Of the others, jcornaz's beancount-parser is a Rust library with no bindings here, robinvdvleuten's Go implementation would need a shim and a module download, and hledger reads the Ledger journal rather than this one and is not installable in this environment without a Haskell toolchain; none of them was used and the search is recorded because rule 2a requires it either way. What lima settles is the part of the claim that was never in doubt and was never established: that the two spellings are one number. Its parser returns the same Decimal for 100.01 and 100.010 and reports the assertion's tolerance as absent in both files, and fractions.Fraction makes them the same rational exactly. So the difference in verdict comes from beancount and from nowhere else, and beancount's own source says how. get_balance_tolerance in beancount/ops/balance.py at 3.2.3 (raw.githubusercontent.com/beancount/beancount/3.2.3/beancount/ops/balance.py) takes expo = balance_entry.amount.number.as_tuple().exponent and, when it is negative, sets tolerance = ONE.scaleb(expo) * options_map["tolerance_multiplier"] * 2 under the comment "Be generous and always allow twice the multiplier on Balance and Pad because the user creates these and the rounding of those balances may often be further off than those used within a single transaction"; where the exponent is not negative it sets the tolerance to zero instead. Executed over generated amounts, the rule runs both ways: an assertion one cent off the posted balance is accepted when written to two places and rejected when written to three, four, five or six, and an assertion written with no decimal point at all is rejected where the identical value written to two places is accepted. The other two claims of the case hold and gain a second reading. The completing posting amount is supplied by beancount's booking and is not in the file, which the Rust parser shows by returning that posting with no amount while the loader returns both postings summing to zero; and an unbalanced journal is an error returned in a list, with the offending transaction still handed on, while the same file is a clean parse to lima because only the arithmetic is wrong. What this changes in P155 is that the tolerance a chain relies on is not declared anywhere in its data: it is inferred from the typography of the number, so reformatting a journal to a consistent number of decimal places silently changes which assertions can fail.

P154 matches two sides of a reconciliation on a normalised key, and case 154 of handoff_guards_v16 records that casefold merges keys that lower keeps apart. Two other runtimes implement the same operation and all three cite the same specification. CPython's Doc/library/stdtypes.rst at tag v3.11.15 (raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.11.15/Doc/library/stdtypes.rst) says of str.casefold that "The casefolding algorithm is described in section 3.13 of the Unicode Standard"; Ruby's doc/case_mapping.rdoc at tag v3_3_6 (raw.githubusercontent.com/ruby/ruby/v3_3_6/doc/case_mapping.rdoc) says its case methods "use full Unicode case mapping" and cites the same section, and documents its option as "+:fold+ (available only for String#downcase, String#downcase!, and Symbol#downcase): Unicode case folding, which is more far-reaching than Unicode case mapping"; PHP's manual lists MB_CASE_FOLD as a mode of mb_convert_case in reference/mbstring/functions/mb-convert-case.xml of the doc-en clone. Executed on generated text the three agree exactly, on the fold and on the lowercase, which is the opposite result from the month arithmetic recorded above: this convention does carry across runtimes, and the merge P154 relies on is a property of the published algorithm rather than of CPython. Two things the case did not say came out of running it. Folding is not a stronger lowercase: for a block of assigned letters the fold is the identity while the lowercase is not, so a key built by folding still carries case that lowercasing would have removed, and all three runtimes do that. And the fold only ever merges, never separates, which is recorded as an invariant of the output over generated words rather than as a comparison. The sharper finding is that the three do not share one Unicode version. The regex module at 2026.9.3 carries its own tables and matches fifty-five characters as \p{Lu} that this Python's unicodedata files as unassigned and its casefold and lower both leave untouched; PHP 8.4.19 folds twenty-seven of those same characters, and the tests establish which by asking the runtime rather than by naming them. So the same deduplication key computed on two sides of a service boundary is not the same key for those letters, silently, and which letters they are moves with the interpreter build rather than with the data. A defect in the oracle itself is worth recording too: Ruby takes both the encoding of its arguments and the encoding of its output from the locale, and with no locale set it folds nothing outside ASCII, so the shim tags its argument as UTF-8 explicitly. Nothing about P154's claim changes; what changes is that the key it computes is portable between languages only for the characters every runtime in the chain already knows.

P158 rolls opportunities up by a declared stage, and case 158 of handoff_guards_v16 records two things: a label the mapping does not cover becomes a missing value with no error, and the rollup reports either three bars or five from the same frame. Both halves were run against polars 1.44.1 and DuckDB 1.5.5, neither of which shares code with pandas 2.2.3. On the mapping, one operation has three answers. pandas documents its own in the Series.map docstring at v2.2.3 (raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/v2.2.3/pandas/core/series.py): "``map`` accepts a ``dict`` or a ``Series``. Values that are not found in the ``dict`` are converted to ``NaN``, unless the dict has a default value (e.g. ``defaultdict``)", and its signature offers no other setting. polars refuses the same call: its replace_strict docstring at tag py-1.44.1 says of the default parameter, "Set values that were not replaced to this value. If no default is specified, (default), an error is raised if any values were not replaced", and lists InvalidOperationError under Raises "If any non-null values in the original column were not replaced, and no `default` was specified". Its other spelling, replace, leaves an uncovered label exactly as it found it and loses nothing. Executed on generated rows the three behaviours are a null, a refusal and an untouched value, and the silent one is the default; asked for the missing value in its own terms, with default=None, polars marks precisely the rows pandas marks. What pandas puts in the gap is a float in a column of text, which polars will not accept as a string column at all, so the damage shows up as a load failure in the next engine rather than as a different number. On the rollup, neither other engine can produce the extra bars: polars groups what is there and the SQL join finds no partner for an uncovered label, and with observed=True pandas agrees with both of them on every generated set of rows, while observed=False reports every declared stage including those no row reached, as a sum of zero that is written exactly like a measured zero. All three engines leave the uncovered amount out of the totals, and they agree on the figure, which is what makes the shortfall hard to see: two independent engines confirm a total that is missing rows. pandas' own documentation at v2.2.3 says this default is going: under observed the frame.py docstring carries ".. deprecated:: 2.2.0" and "The default value of ``False`` is deprecated and will change to ``True`` in a future version of pandas." So the five-bar chart P158 can draw today is a behaviour the library has already announced it will stop producing, and the proof does not record which of the two it depends on.

P151 binds a DOCX template and case 151 of handoff_guards_v16 records that the binding escapes nothing by default and that a StrictUndefined environment does not turn escaping on. The second implementation is the same template language in another runtime. nunjucks 3.2.4 is JavaScript; its package.json at tag v3.2.4 (raw.githubusercontent.com/mozilla/nunjucks/v3.2.4/package.json) lists a-sync-waterfall, asap and commander and nothing from Python. The two projects choose opposite defaults for the same operation and each documents its own. jinja2 3.1.6's Environment signature at tag 3.1.6 (raw.githubusercontent.com/pallets/jinja/3.1.6/src/jinja2/environment.py) reads autoescape: t.Union[bool, t.Callable[[t.Optional[str]], bool]] = False, and its docstring says only what happens "If set to ``True``", never stating the default in prose; nunjucks' docs/api.md at v3.2.4 lists "**autoescape** *(default: true)* controls if output with dangerous characters are escaped automatically". Executed on generated values drawn from the characters jinja2's own escaping changes, nunjucks escapes every one and jinja2 escapes none, and turning nunjucks' flag off reproduces jinja2's default exactly. So whether a rendered document is safe depends on which runtime rendered it, and neither library is doing anything undocumented. Two further things came out of running it. Both engines can be told to refuse an absent variable, and in both the setting is independent of the escaping: jinja2 with StrictUndefined still does not escape and nunjucks with throwOnUndefined still does, so the environment a chain reaches for when it wants strictness is not the environment that makes the output safe, in either runtime. And when both are escaping they do not produce the same text: over the ninety-five printable characters the two agree on ninety-three and differ on two, the double quote, which jinja2 writes as &#34; and nunjucks as &quot;, and the backslash, which jinja2 leaves alone and nunjucks writes as &#92;. Both are safe and the bytes differ, so a rendered document produced in one runtime does not match a byte comparison against the same document produced in the other. Which two characters those are is established in the tests by asking both engines about every printable character, not by naming them. What this changes in P151 is that the escaping default is not a fact about the template language, and neither is the rendered output: both belong to the implementation, and the proof names neither.

P152 joins each invoice line to its order line with pandas 2.2.3's merge(validate="many_to_one", indicator=True) and the chain is required to retain unmatched lines; case 152 of handoff_guards_v16 types sixteen expectations about what comes back. Two engines that share no code with pandas answer the same questions: polars 1.44.1, whose py-polars/pyproject.toml at tag py-1.44.1 (raw.githubusercontent.com/pola-rs/polars/py-1.44.1/py-polars/pyproject.toml) declares the single dependency polars-runtime-32 and keeps pandas among the optional extras, and DuckDB 1.5.5, a C++ engine whose Python distribution declares no required dependency at all. On the join itself the three agree exactly, over generated order lines and generated references drawn from a disjoint range so that the losing region is constructed rather than filtered for: the inner join keeps the same invoice lines in all three, and what pandas' outer join marks left_only is precisely what the inner join dropped, so the loss is the join and not the library. The indicator that would report it cannot report it, because pandas' merge docstring at v2.2.3 (raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/v2.2.3/pandas/core/frame.py) gives the column "left_only" for observations whose merge key only appears in the left DataFrame and "both" if the observation's merge key is found in both DataFrames, and on an inner join no row can be anything but both, so the flag takes one value however many lines were dropped. The cardinality check is implemented twice and documented in nearly the same words: pandas says of validate that "many_to_one" or "m:1" means "check if merge keys are unique in right dataset", and polars' join docstring at py-1.44.1 (raw.githubusercontent.com/pola-rs/polars/py-1.44.1/py-polars/src/polars/dataframe/frame.py) says of m:1 "Many-to-one. Check if join keys are unique in right dataset."; executed, both refuse a repeated order line, both accept a repeated invoice line, and on the accepted side they return the same rows. Where they part is the missing key. pandas' merge docstring carries the warning "If both key columns contain rows where the key is a null value, those rows will be matched against each other. This is different from usual SQL join behaviour and can lead to unexpected results", and executed it is a full cross product: invoices with no order reference match every order line with no key. polars, whose docstring says of nulls_equal "Join on null values. By default null values will never produce matches", returns nothing, and so does DuckDB, which is to say that the usual SQL join behaviour pandas contrasts itself with is the second engine this same chain reads its workbook with; told to treat nulls as equal, polars reproduces pandas exactly, so this is a default and not a capability. The same difference reaches the guard: with every order line missing, pandas' validate="many_to_one" raises MergeError because it counts two missing keys as one key twice, while polars' validate="m:1" passes and returns what the unvalidated join returns, so the cardinality check P152 relies on fires or does not fire according to which engine holds the frame, on data neither engine considers malformed. Two smaller results follow the same shape. A group whose amounts are all missing totals zero in both dataframe engines and nothing in SQL, and each documents its own answer: pandas' groupby sum takes min_count=0, whose text at v2.2.3 (raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/v2.2.3/pandas/core/groupby/groupby.py) reads "The required number of valid values to perform the operation. If fewer than ``min_count`` non-NA values are present the result will be NA"; polars' Expr.sum docstring at py-1.44.1 says "If there are no non-null values, then the output is `0`"; DuckDB's aggregates page says sum "Calculates the sum of all non-null values in `arg`" and that "All general aggregate functions except `count` return `NULL` on empty groups". duckdb.org is blocked by the egress proxy here, so that page and the typecasting page were read in the duckdb-web repository at commit 6f6cd1659f0e2ddd1965b1d3f1833e7fc512e7ac, whose _config.yml records the current documentation version as 1.5.5, at docs/current/sql/functions/aggregates.md and docs/current/sql/data_types/typecasting.md. Asking pandas for min_count=1 moves it onto SQL's answer exactly, and a total over no amounts at all is not currency in the first place: from a column of Decimals pandas returns a plain integer zero, with no scale and no quantize, so the next comparison against a decimal tolerance is a mixed comparison rather than a decimal one. That tolerance is the sharpest of the four findings. The proof's evidence line claims four signed price-boundary cases confirm the 0.25 USD tolerance, and the case types Decimal('0.25') == 0.25 as true and Decimal('0.1') == 0.1 as false. CPython's decimal documentation at tag v3.11.15 (raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.11.15/Doc/library/decimal.rst) says "it is possible to use Python's comparison operators to compare a Decimal instance x with another number y. This avoids confusing results when doing equality comparisons between numbers of different types", and fractions.Fraction, holding both as exact rationals, confirms the comparison is exact for every hundredth from one cent to two dollars. Eight of those two hundred hundredths are a float exactly; on a hundred of them the nearest double is above the amount and on ninety-two it is below, and that decides the boundary, because where the difference between ordered and billed is exactly the declared tolerance the float spelling of that tolerance accepts it in the first region and refuses it in the second, while the decimal spelling accepts it in both. Twenty-five hundredths, the tolerance the proof names, is one of the eight, so the proof's own boundary cases are the ones that could not have shown this. And the same comparison inside the engine the chain also uses gives the opposite answer: DuckDB reports that a DECIMAL can be cast implicitly to a DOUBLE and not the reverse, its typecasting page says combination casting "occurs for comparisons (`=` / `<` / `>`)", and it therefore rounds the exact amount to the nearest double before comparing, calling equal the hundred and ninety-two pairs Python calls different while still calling different a double that is not the nearest one. What this changes in P152 is that neither the retention of unmatched lines, nor the cardinality guard, nor the tolerance is a property of the data: each is a property of the engine that holds the frame and of how the tolerance was spelled, and the proof names neither.

P153 accumulates stock with pandas 2.2.3's groupby and cumsum after ordering the entries with sort_values, and case 153 of handoff_guards_v16 types the running balances, the tie order and the deduplication by hand. Three independent implementations of a running total answer the first question and agree: polars 1.44.1's cum_sum in Rust, itertools.accumulate, which is a C loop inside CPython and shares no code with either dataframe library, and pandas itself produce the same run for the same order, and the closing balance is the same whichever order the same movements arrive in. The lowest point of that run is not: over generated receipts and issues, putting the receipts first keeps the run above the first receipt and putting the issues first takes it down to the whole issued quantity, so P153's rejection of negative running stock fires on an ordering the primitive does not impose. Where a quantity is missing the three part company, and so does the fourth. pandas' cumsum takes skipna=True, documented at v2.2.3 (raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/v2.2.3/pandas/core/generic.py) as "Exclude NA/null values. If an entire row/column is NA, the result will be NA", and executed it leaves the gap missing and resumes the balance after it as though the gap were zero. numpy 2.4.6's cumsum (raw.githubusercontent.com/numpy/numpy/v2.4.6/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py), whose Notes mention only that "Arithmetic is modular when using integer types, and no error is raised on overflow", carries the NaN to the end of the ledger and so does itertools.accumulate, and so does polars when the gap is written as a NaN; polars when the same gap is written as a null resumes exactly as pandas does, and its cum_sum docstring at py-1.44.1 (raw.githubusercontent.com/pola-rs/polars/py-1.44.1/py-polars/src/polars/expr/expr.py) says nothing about missing values at all, documenting only an overflow cast. So one missing quantity either counts as zero or voids every balance after it, and which of the two a chain gets depends on the library and on whether the gap arrived as a null or as a NaN; pandas' own skipna=False reproduces the voided run exactly, which is the lever the proof does not name. The sort is the sharpest of the three. pandas' sort_values docstring at v2.2.3 (raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/v2.2.3/pandas/core/frame.py) offers kind as "{'quicksort', 'mergesort', 'heapsort', 'stable'}, default 'quicksort'" and says "`mergesort` and `stable` are the only stable algorithms", and P153 sorts without naming one. Asked for a stable sort, pandas, CPython's own sorted -- whose sorting howto at tag v3.11.15 (raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.11.15/Doc/howto/sorting.rst) says "Sorts are guaranteed to be stable. That means that when multiple records have the same key, their original order is preserved" -- and polars with maintain_order=True, documented at py-1.44.1 (raw.githubusercontent.com/pola-rs/polars/py-1.44.1/py-polars/src/polars/dataframe/frame.py) as "Whether the order should be maintained if elements are equal", put tied entries in the order they arrived, on every generated ledger. The default does not, and the threshold is the finding: over generated ledgers of two to sixteen entries whose day codes are drawn from a range of four, so that ties are forced, the default agrees with all three on every example, and from seventeen entries upward it disagrees on every example, keeping the same rows and moving them. P153's own evidence line describes eighteen declared ledger entries, one past the point at which this becomes visible, so the fixture that demonstrates the chain is on the far side of a threshold the proof does not mention and a smaller one would have shown nothing. The deduplication is the quiet one. Every receipt reference in the generated frames appears twice with quantities that differ by a generated amount, and pandas' drop_duplicates(subset=...), polars' unique(subset=..., keep='first') and DuckDB 1.5.5's DISTINCT ON keep the same first row and discard the disagreeing one without a word, so the silence is the operation rather than the library; deduplicating on the reference and the quantity together keeps more rows than deduplicating on the reference alone, which is the only signal any of the three gives that the discarded rows were not duplicates. What this changes in P153 is that the balance figure is the one thing that does not depend on the ordering: the negative-stock rejection, the order of tied entries and the treatment of a gap each depend on a default, and the proof names none of them.

P156 parses declared service intervals from ISO 8601 text, requires an offset, and rounds the billable amount to cents; case 156 of handoff_guards_v16 types the spellings the parse accepts and the cents the two rounding modes produce. Two other runtimes read the same text through their own implementations, reached by the shims iso_stamp_oracle.rb and iso_stamp_oracle.php, and each of the three documents a different scope for the same standard. CPython's datetime.fromisoformat at tag v3.11.15 (raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.11.15/Doc/library/datetime.rst) is documented as returning "a datetime corresponding to a date_string in any valid ISO 8601 format, with the following exceptions", of which the first is "Time zone offsets may have fractional seconds" and the third is "Fractional hours and minutes are not supported", and its own examples parse both 20111104 and 2011-11-04. Ruby 3.3.6's Time.iso8601 is alias iso8601 xmlschema in lib/time.rb at tag v3_3_6 (raw.githubusercontent.com/ruby/ruby/v3_3_6/lib/time.rb), documented as parsing "a dateTime defined by the XML Schema", "a restricted version of the format defined by ISO 8601", raising ArgumentError otherwise, and writing "CCYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssTZD" "where TZD is Z or [+-]hh:mm". PHP 8.4.19's DateTimeImmutable takes the formats tabulated in reference/datetime/formats.xml of the php/doc-en clone at commit d8de774ae203bccf3ffe02895d8c8fc754377451, whose ISO8601 Notations table lists an "Eight digit year, month and day" and whose tzcorrection grammar is "GMT"? [+-] hh ":"? MM?. Executed over generated moments and generated offsets, the extended spelling with a whole-minute offset is one instant in all three, which is what makes the rest divergences of the spelling rather than of the runtimes. A timestamp with no offset is naive in CPython and an instant in the other two, which attach their own configured zone to text that names none, so the entry the chain has to reject separately is already decided elsewhere. The same moment written without separators, and a date with no time at all, are read by CPython and by PHP -- the date becoming a midnight nobody wrote down -- and refused by Ruby. The sharpest is the offset that is not a whole number of minutes, of which case 156 types one instance: CPython reads it and keeps it, Ruby refuses it, and PHP reads it correctly, reporting through getOffset the same number of seconds CPython reports, and then cannot write it back, because the timestamp it formats carries an offset that a second reading of PHP's own output does not agree with. The seconds field is outside PHP's own documented tzcorrection grammar and is honoured on input and dropped on output, silently. Sub-second precision divides them too: CPython and PHP report the same microsecond and have no field below it, while Ruby's parse holds a nanosecond count its own microsecond accessor cannot express, so two timestamps that are equal in Python are not equal in Ruby and the digits that separate them are ones Python never saw. The rounding is a smaller finding of the same kind. The chain rounds in Python, whose decimal default is half to even, and reads the figures back through a workbook and a SQL engine; DuckDB 1.5.5, whose numeric page in the duckdb-web checkout at commit 6f6cd1659f0e2ddd1965b1d3f1833e7fc512e7ac says of round only "Round to `s` decimal places. Values `s < 0` are allowed." and does not say which way a tie goes, rounds a decimal column half away from zero on every generated half cent, which is Python's ROUND_HALF_UP and not Python's default, so the cent computed in Python and the cent the same figure gets in SQL differ on exactly the ties the two Python modes split. The engine does not have one answer either: on some of those same ties, rounding the figure in a double column gives a different cent from rounding it in a decimal column, inside one engine, on one number, and which ties those are is settled by asking the engine both ways rather than by predicting it from the binary value. What this changes in P156 is that neither the acceptance of a timestamp nor the instant it denotes nor the cent it is billed at is a property of the text: each belongs to the runtime that read it and to the column type it was written into, and the proof names one runtime and one mode.

P160 builds a bill of materials with NetworkX 3.6.1's DiGraph.add_edge and expands it into gross requirements, and case 160 of handoff_guards_v16 types the edge counts, the quantities and the path results. igraph 1.0.0, a C library with its own graph implementation whose Python distribution requires only texttable at runtime and names networkx solely under its test extra, and a recursive query in DuckDB 1.5.5 answer the same questions, and where the declarations are unique all three agree exactly: over generated acyclic bills, NetworkX's all_simple_paths with math.prod, igraph's get_all_simple_paths and a DuckDB WITH RECURSIVE expansion that never enumerates a path produce the same gross requirement, so the arithmetic of a nested assembly is the operation rather than the library. Four things are not. Declaring the same parent and child twice stores one edge in NetworkX, whose add_edge docstring at tag networkx-3.6.1 (raw.githubusercontent.com/networkx/networkx/networkx-3.6.1/networkx/classes/digraph.py) says "Adding an edge that already exists updates the edge data", and two parallel edges in igraph, which keeps both quantities, one edge for every declaration in the file; the quantity NetworkX keeps is the last one igraph kept, so nothing is corrupted and the same file simply calls for different amounts of material in the two libraries. The acyclicity check is eager in one and lazy in the other: NetworkX's topological_sort is documented at that tag (raw.githubusercontent.com/networkx/networkx/networkx-3.6.1/networkx/algorithms/dag.py) as returning "a generator of nodes in topologically sorted order" which raises NetworkXUnfeasible "If `G` is not a directed acyclic graph (DAG)", and executed on a generated ring the exception arrives only when the generator is consumed, while igraph's topological_sorting raises at the call; the two predicates agree that the ring is cyclic, so the whole difference is when the refusal arrives, and a chain that calls topological_sort without consuming it has checked nothing. Asked for the paths from an item to itself, NetworkX returns one path, the item alone, and igraph returns none, and the product of no quantities is one -- which math and numpy agree on -- so NetworkX turns a demand for an assembly into a requirement for that same assembly at the demanded quantity out of a graph that declares no such edge. And the two ends of one query are not treated alike: an item the graph has never heard of raises NodeNotFound as a source and returns quietly as a target, because all_simple_paths delegates to all_simple_edge_paths, whose target parameter is documented as "Single node or iterable of nodes at which to end path" and which, at that tag, raises only when the source is absent and otherwise falls through to "targets = set(target)" when the target is not in the graph, so a missing part number is not rejected but reinterpreted as a collection of target nodes, which for a part number is its characters, and matches nothing. What comes back is indistinguishable from the answer for a part that is in the graph and cannot be reached, which is the comparison the test makes; igraph refuses both ends with a ValueError. What this changes in P160 is that the requirement figure is reproducible across three engines while the graph it is computed from is not: how many edges a repeated declaration makes, whether an item requires itself, when a cycle is refused and whether an unknown part is an error all belong to the library, and the proof names one library.

P163 locates declared passages in a meeting PDF with PyMuPDF's Page.search_for, checks the recovered characters with Page.get_textbox, and marks them with add_highlight_annot and Annot.set_info; case 163 of handoff_guards_v17 types the hit counts, the recovered strings and the annotation fields by hand. P163 pins PyMuPDF 1.26.6 and the hardening environment runs 1.28.2, so everything below was read and executed at 1.28.2. The second implementation is PDFium, reached through pypdfium2 5.13.0, which binds libpdfium 153.0.7999.0 here and declares no runtime dependency of any kind in its published metadata at the 5.13.0 tag: its pyproject.toml carries a build-system table and PEP 735 dependency groups and no [project] table at all, and the [metadata] section of its setup.cfg declares none (raw.githubusercontent.com/pypdfium2-team/pypdfium2/5.13.0/pyproject.toml and the setup.cfg beside it), so rule 2a's requirement that the oracle not wrap the library under test is settled from its own dependency list. The annotations are read a second way with pypdf 6.17.0, a pure-Python parser of the PDF object model whose only declared dependency is typing_extensions on Python below 3.11 (raw.githubusercontent.com/py-pdf/pypdf/6.17.0/pyproject.toml). pdfplumber was the other candidate and was set aside for this cluster, because its search is a regular expression over pdfminer.six's extracted text rather than an engine's own search, and because it is already the oracle for the character-level extraction recorded above. Every primitive was read at its pinned version before use: PyMuPDF's search_for and get_textbox in docs/page.rst at tag 1.28.2 (raw.githubusercontent.com/pymupdf/PyMuPDF/1.28.2/docs/page.rst), pypdfium2's PdfTextPage.search and get_text_bounded in src/pypdfium2/_helpers/textpage.py at tag 5.13.0, and pypdf's documented way of reading annotations in docs/user/reading-pdf-annotations.md at tag 6.17.0. Over generated words written to the page by PyMuPDF itself, the two engines agree exactly where the proof needs them to: a phrase that lies on one line and never occurs twice in a row is found the same number of times by both, PDFium's matched character range is the phrase, and PyMuPDF's rectangle read back with get_textbox holds the phrase and nothing else. Four things diverge, and PyMuPDF documents three of them itself. Contiguous occurrences are one hit, because "the search logic regards **contiguous multiple occurrences** of *needle* as one", so a word written twice with nothing between gives one rectangle in PyMuPDF and two matches in PDFium; one highlight then covers two quotations, and the number of located passages belongs to the engine rather than to the page. The case-insensitivity is ASCII only, which the same page states: "Upper / lower case is ignored, but only works for ASCII characters: For example, "COMPÉTENCES" will not be found if needle is "compétences" -- "compÉtences" however will." PDFium folds the accented letter too, so one needle finds one passage in one engine and two in the other, and P163's recorded claim that "ASCII case-insensitivity in the library search is constrained by an explicit exact-text comparison" is true of a candidate set that another reader of the same file would not produce. A phrase that crosses a line break is not one hit either: PyMuPDF documents that "if parts of *needle* occur on more than one line, then a separate item is generated for each these parts", while PDFium returns the single character range that carries the whole phrase across the break, so highlighting the first returned rectangle, as the chain does, marks the first line of a wrapped quotation and nothing of the second. The fourth divergence is the rectangle itself, and it is the one that reaches the exact-text check. At a line gap of twelve to fourteen points for the eleven-point default text, get_textbox over the rectangle search_for returned recovers the line underneath as well; at sixteen points and above it does not. PDFium's bounded read of the same rectangle returns only the matched line at both spacings, and so does PyMuPDF's own get_text with a clip, whose documented rule is that "a character becomes part of the output, if its bbox is contained in `clip`" -- a note attached to get_text, while get_textbox is documented only as "It is based on dedicated code (changed in v1.19.0)". Two primitives of one library therefore disagree about what lies inside one rectangle, and the one the chain uses is the one that disagrees with PDFium and with the documented rule; what it costs is a false rejection, because an exact comparison against those recovered characters throws away a passage that was located correctly whenever the source is set at ordinary single line spacing. The annotation half of the chain agrees. Over generated comments and author names, the content, the author and the subtype written by set_info come back identically from PyMuPDF and from pypdf without Annot.update ever being called, so update is not what persists them; that is what case 163 typed, and it now rests on two readers. What this changes in P163 is that neither the number of passages found nor the verdict of the exact-text check is a property of the document. Both belong to MuPDF's search and to the line spacing of the page it ran on, and the proof's "Three exact passages" and "Six malformed or mismatched requests are rejected, including a case-changed phrase" are counts from one engine on one layout.

P164 looks up misspelled source words with rapidfuzz's process.extract at score_cutoff=1 and limit=None, scored by DamerauLevenshtein.distance; case 164 of handoff_guards_v17 types the returned words, the distances, the truncation and the six words the default limit drops. Rule 2a's search for a second implementation of the metric returned fastDamerauLevenshtein, pyxDamerauLevenshtein, textdistance and jellyfish as candidates that do not build on rapidfuzz, and nothing needed installing: nltk 3.10.3 was already present, and its published setup.py at tag v3.10.3 (raw.githubusercontent.com/nltk/nltk/v3.10.3/setup.py) declares an install_requires of defusedxml, click, joblib, regex and tqdm and nothing else, so its edit_distance is a pure-Python implementation of the same metric sharing no backend with the C++ one. The Levenshtein distribution that is installed here was rejected as an oracle rather than used: its pyproject.toml at tag v0.27.4 (raw.githubusercontent.com/rapidfuzz/Levenshtein/v0.27.4/pyproject.toml) declares dependencies = ["rapidfuzz >= 3.9.0, < 4.0.0"], so it wraps the library under test, and python-Levenshtein in turn requires it. rapidfuzz's own sources were read at tag v3.14.6 for every claim below -- process.extract in src/rapidfuzz/process_py.py, the two metrics in src/rapidfuzz/distance/DamerauLevenshtein_py.py and OSA_py.py -- and nltk's edit_distance in nltk/metrics/distance.py at tag v3.10.3. The metric agrees: over generated text, rapidfuzz's DamerauLevenshtein and nltk's edit_distance with transpositions enabled return the same number, so P164's one-edit bound now rests on two implementations. Four things about the lookup do not follow from the metric, and each is a default.
