The scorer is one of several in the same module, and rapidfuzz's docstrings carry the divergence as their own examples: DamerauLevenshtein.distance("CA", "ABC") is 2 while OSA.distance("CA", "ABC") is 3, because the restricted metric may not edit a substring it has already transposed. nltk's transposition mode is the unrestricted one and answers with DamerauLevenshtein, and plain Levenshtein charges two edits for the adjacent swap the chain exists to catch, so a one-edit bound keeps a transposed misspelling under the scorer P164 names and drops it under the scorer beside it. The cutoff is sharper still, because one number means opposite things: process.extract documents that "When an edit distance is used this represents the maximum edit distance and matches with a `distance > score_cutoff` are ignored. When a normalized edit distance is used this represents the minimal similarity and matches with a `similarity < score_cutoff` are ignored", and executed with one as the cutoff, DamerauLevenshtein.distance keeps the words within one edit, DamerauLevenshtein.similarity keeps a strictly larger set that contains them, and normalized_similarity keeps only the words nltk also places at the query's distance from itself. Swapping a scorer for its neighbour therefore turns the declared bound into a pass-through or into an equality test, and nothing raises. The limit is what case 164 is named for. It is documented as the "maximum amount of results to return. None can be passed to disable this behavior. Default is 5", and equal scores are ordered by source position -- "When multiple choices have the same similarity, they are sorted by their index" -- so on a list of distinct words at a one-edit bound, where only the query itself can score zero, every word after the first is tied. Executed, the truncated answer is a prefix of the full one and the first word dropped carries the same distance as the last word kept, on every generated example where the limit binds at all: the cut is settled by where a word happens to sit in the source index. The processor is the fourth: it defaults to None, described as "Optional callable that is used to preprocess the strings before comparing them. Default is None, which deactivates this behaviour", so a query typed in capitals matches nothing at a one-edit bound, which nltk confirms by returning the same enlarged distances, and passing str.lower recovers exactly the words the lowercase query returns. What this changes in P164 is that its claim to retain "Every word within the declared one-edit bound ... including tied alternatives" is a property of the two arguments the chain passes and not of the lookup. Under the library's own defaults the same call returns five words rather than all of them, nothing at all for a capitalised query, and a different set entirely for the scorer next to the one named, and in each case the answer has the same shape and raises nothing.

P168 reads dated currency rates out of a JSON fixture and converts expense amounts with Decimal; case 168 of handoff_guards_v17 types the parsed rate, the leading twenty characters of its exact binary value, the converted cents and the NaN and Infinity results. Two more implementations of the same format now answer the same documents. orjson 3.12.0 is a Rust parser whose Cargo.toml at tag 3.12.0 (raw.githubusercontent.com/ijl/orjson/3.12.0/Cargo.toml) depends on associative-cache, bytecount, encoding_rs, itoap, jiff-core, once_cell, pyo3-ffi, simdutf8, unwinding, xxhash-rust and zmij, no Python package among them, so it reimplements the format rather than wrapping the module under test; V8's JSON.parse is reached under node v22.22.2 through the shim json_number_oracle.js, and its parser was read in deps/v8/src/json/json-parser.cc of the node checkout at tag v22.22.2. CPython's own documentation was read at tag v3.11.15 (raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.11.15/Doc/library/json.rst) and orjson's behaviour in its README at tag 3.12.0. The three parsers agree on the number: for a generated rate written with one decimal place, the C scanner, the Rust parser and V8 return the same double, which is what makes everything below a property of the format rather than of one reader. What that double is is not what the file says. One decimal place that is not a half is never a binary fraction, so the rate comes back as a different rational number, which fractions.Fraction reads off both sides exactly -- the 1.1 of the fixture is 2476979795053773/2251799813685248 once parsed -- and the declared digits survive only when parse_float is passed, documented as "*parse_float*, if specified, will be called with the string of every JSON float to be decoded. By default, this is equivalent to ``float(num_str)``." The value that arrives by default cannot enter the chain's own arithmetic at all, because a Decimal refuses to multiply a float, which is the type error case 168 records. Which rates survive is decided by the denominator and not by the length: every multiple of one two-hundred-and-fifty-sixth passes through the double unchanged in value and in spelling, while a rate written to eighteen or more decimal places comes back from both parsers as a number whose own spelling is shorter than the one declared, with nothing raised and no field recording that digits were dropped. Two edges of the format remain, and only one of them is a divergence. The standard library states its own extensions: "This module does not comply with the RFC in a strict fashion, implementing some extensions that are valid JavaScript but not valid JSON. In particular: - Infinite and NaN number values are accepted and output; - Repeated names within an object are accepted, and only the value of the last name-value pair is used." The first is local to it. json.loads reads NaN, Infinity and -Infinity as floats, and parse_constant hands back the literal that was written, which is how the test recovers the value without one being typed; orjson raises JSONDecodeError, documented as "It raises `JSONDecodeError` if given an invalid type or invalid JSON. This includes if the input contains `NaN`, `Infinity`, or `-Infinity`, which the standard library allows, but is not valid JSON"; and V8 raises a SyntaxError, which reaches the tests as a non-zero exit from the shim. The standard library calls these extensions "valid JavaScript", and the JavaScript runtime's own JSON parser refuses all three, listing "Infinity" and "NaN" in json-parser.cc among "The special cases ... being passed to the parse method". A rates file carrying one of them therefore loads in this chain and is rejected by the next reader of the same bytes, and P168's evidence line, which counts "nonfinite rates" among its rejected inputs, is rejecting them with a check of its own rather than with the parser. The second extension is not a divergence: orjson and V8 also accept a repeated name and also keep the last value, so a document that declares one currency twice is accepted by every parser tried here and the earlier rate is unrecoverable from all of them. What this changes in P168 is that the rate the chain converts with is the declared rate only when the file writes it as a string or the loader passes parse_float, and that the format's extensions cut both ways: the chain's nonfinite guard is doing work no parser does for it, while its duplicate-name guard is stricter than every parser it could be compared with.

P161 requires one explicit classification for every prior journal transaction and checks that requirement with a pandera schema followed by a pandas Index comparison; case 161 of handoff_guards_v17 types the accepted row count, the identifier each refusal names and the emptiness of the index difference. Two other implementations of the same declared rule now answer the same lists. The jsonschema package 4.26.0 implements the JSON Schema keywords enum and uniqueItems, and its _keywords.py at tag v4.26.0 (raw.githubusercontent.com/python-jsonschema/jsonschema/v4.26.0/jsonschema/_keywords.py) yields for uniqueItems a ValidationError against the whole instance, "{instance!r} has non-unique elements", and for enum one against the element; DuckDB 1.5.5 enforces the same two things as table constraints, documented in the duckdb-web checkout at commit 6f6cd1659f0e2ddd1965b1d3f1833e7fc512e7ac (docs/current/sql/constraints.md) as "Check constraints allow you to specify an arbitrary Boolean expression. Any columns that *do not* satisfy this expression violate the constraint" and "Primary key or unique constraints define a column, or set of columns, that are a unique identifier for a row in the table." pandera's own source was read at tag v0.33.1 (raw.githubusercontent.com/unionai-oss/pandera/v0.33.1/pandera/api/pandas/components.py), whose Column documents ":param unique: whether column values should be unique" and a report_duplicates setting whose default is "`all`: (default) report all duplicates". Over generated lists drawn from the four declared identifiers and two undeclared ones, the three engines accept and refuse exactly the same lists, so the rule P161 declares does not depend on the validator that happens to check it. What each of them says about a refusal does depend on it. pandera names the repeated identifier and every row it sits on, and polars 1.44.1 finds the same value and the same rows independently with is_duplicated; the jsonschema uniqueItems failure carries an empty absolute_path, because the keyword fails against the array and not against an element, so its structured error names no identifier at all; DuckDB's documented refusal names the value and not the row, in the form "Duplicate key "id: 1" violates primary key constraint". For an undeclared identifier the two structured reports agree exactly -- pandera's failing index and the absolute_path of the enum error are the same row -- so the difference is between the two keywords rather than between the libraries, and P161's need to name an identifier is met by one of the two checks and not by the other. The coverage half is the finding the case is named for, and it is now executed on generated postings rather than typed. The step is pd.Index(declared).symmetric_difference(pd.Index(posted)), and a set operation deduplicates before it compares: a frame that posts one journal twice while covering every declared journal produces exactly the same empty difference as the exact frame, so the comparison cannot tell them apart. That is not a pandas defect. DuckDB's EXCEPT answers the same way on the same lists in both directions, which places the blindness in the set operation itself, and the repeat is visible only to a uniqueness constraint, which all three engines offer and only one of which this chain asks for. What this changes in P161 is that its claim to "account for all 18 postings from the P155 journal exactly once" rests entirely on the schema's unique=True: the index comparison standing beside it would pass unchanged if one journal were classified twice, and the classification totals it feeds would then double-count that transaction without any step in the chain saying so.

P170 computes a whole-bundle break-even volume as (Decimal(fixed) / Decimal(contribution)).to_integral_value(ROUND_CEILING); case 170 of handoff_guards_v17 types that volume, the profit either side of it and the two roundings of a negative contribution. Three other implementations of the same ceiling now answer the same figures: fractions.Fraction, whose quotient is exact and whose ceiling is CPython's math.ceil on that rational; IEEE double arithmetic through Python's own float and numpy 2.4.6; and DuckDB 1.5.5. The rounding modes were read at tag v3.11.15 (raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.11.15/Doc/library/decimal.rst), which defines ROUND_CEILING as "Round towards ``Infinity``." and ROUND_UP as "Round away from zero.", and gives the module an "alterable precision (defaulting to 28 places)"; DuckDB's operators were read in the duckdb-web checkout at commit 6f6cd1659f0e2ddd1965b1d3f1833e7fc512e7ac, whose numeric-functions page tabulates `/` as "Float division" and whose Division and Modulo Operators section describes the operators for FLOAT, DOUBLE and integer operands and says nothing at all about DECIMAL. Over generated contributions from one cent to twenty dollars and fixed costs built as an exact whole number of bundles, decimal and Fraction return the same volume on every example, and it is the bundle count the cost was built from. The other two do not. The same quotient in binary floating point never returns fewer bundles and returns one more on about an eighth of the generated counts, because the fixed cost and the contribution are each inexact as doubles and the quotient of the two falls just above the whole number it should equal; nothing raises, and the surplus bundle is indistinguishable in the answer from a genuine part-bundle remainder. DuckDB gives that same answer, and why is worth stating separately: executed on two DECIMAL operands its `/` returns a DOUBLE, so the ceiling of a DECIMAL quotient and the ceiling of a DOUBLE quotient are one number in that engine. A break-even recomputed in SQL from the same declared figures is therefore not a decimal calculation whatever the column types say, and the engine's own documentation does not tell a reader so, because it documents division for floats and integers only. Two edge cases separate the four further. A product that contributes nothing has no break-even volume: decimal raises DivisionByZero and Fraction raises ZeroDivisionError, while numpy and DuckDB both answer with an infinity and no exception, so whether the unanswerable case arrives as a refusal or as a number is settled by which library the figure passed through. And a contribution below zero still divides. Its quotient is negative, and that is where the two roundings part: ROUND_CEILING moves toward positive infinity while ROUND_UP moves away from zero, so they differ by one bundle, and Fraction's exact ceiling confirms that ROUND_CEILING is the one that moves toward zero here. The volume P170's ROUND_CEILING returns is the one at which the product is still losing money and the volume ROUND_UP returns is the one at which it is not, so on a negative contribution the declared rounding answers the opposite question. What this changes in P170 is that the exactness it relies on belongs to the decimal and Fraction implementations alone: the same question asked in the float arithmetic its own volume range is enumerated with, or asked of a SQL engine, is answered one bundle high on about an eighth of the exact cases, and the rounding the proof declares is the right one only while the contribution is positive, which is a condition the chain computes rather than declares.

P166 edits a date in a native ODS workbook and reads the sheet back, expecting the formula that depends on it to follow; case 166 of handoff_guards_v17 types the date before and after, the surviving formula and its cached result. Two independent readers of the same bytes now answer instead. python-calamine 0.8.2 is, in its own words at the v0.8.2 tag (raw.githubusercontent.com/dimastbk/python-calamine/v0.8.2/README.md), a "Python binding for beautiful Rust's library for reading excel and odf file - calamine", and its pyproject.toml at that tag carries a [project] table with no dependencies field at all, so nothing of odfpy is under it; libxml2 through lxml 6.1.3 reads content.xml straight out of the zip as a third view. odfpy's own reader was read at tag release-1.4.1 (raw.githubusercontent.com/eea/odfpy/release-1.4.1/odf/teletype.py), where extractText is documented as returning "the text, with tabs, spaces, and newlines correctly evaluated", "unwrapping" <text:s>, <text:tab>, and <text:line-break> elements along the way -- a reader of the displayed paragraph that never consults the typed attribute beside it. On a cell whose typed date and displayed paragraph were written together, all three agree on the day, over generated dates from 1900 to 2100. An edit does not keep them together. Setting office:date-value, which is the attribute that carries the value, moves the day python-calamine reports and leaves the text:p paragraph exactly as it was, and lxml finds both of them sitting in content.xml afterwards: one cell, two readers, two different days, nothing raised and neither reader wrong. The formula cell is the same story one step further on. Moving the date it refers to changes neither its table:formula nor its office:value, and python-calamine returns the same number it returned before the edit, which is the difference of the dates as they were and not as they are. Nothing in the package recomputes anything, and a reader that sees only values -- which is what to_python returns -- cannot tell that the number it has is stale. What this changes in P166 is that "date edit and formula recalculation", the chain's own description of the step, is one operation the package performs and one it does not: the edit is real, the recalculation is a spreadsheet application's work, and a workbook written this way carries a displayed date and a derived figure that both still answer the question asked before the edit. Which of the two a downstream reader sees is decided by whether it reads values or text.

P165 converts Word files to native ODT and then, in the chain's own words, "reload ODT blocks and compare paragraph order and every table cell"; case 165 of handoff_guards_v17 types the expanded whitespace of three paragraphs, the two paragraph counts and the welded text of a table. A second ODF library now answers the same document. Rule 2a's search ran two queries, "odfdo python OpenDocument library independent of odfpy lpod-python fork" and "node.js library extract text from ODT OpenDocument content.xml npm", and turned up odfdo and the abandoned Python 2 lpod-python on the Python side and officeparser, textract, extract-text and node-odt on npm. odfdo 3.25.0 was installed and used, because its lineage and its dependency list can both be read at the pinned tag: its README at tag v3.25.0 (raw.githubusercontent.com/jdum/odfdo/v3.25.0/README.md) says "`odfdo` is a derivative work of the former `lpod-python` project.", and its pyproject.toml at that tag declares dependencies of lxml and typing-extensions and nothing else, so no part of odfpy is underneath it. odfpy's own extractText was read at tag release-1.4.1 (raw.githubusercontent.com/eea/odfpy/release-1.4.1/odf/teletype.py), whose module docstring says that getTextContent "won't extract or create the appropriate <text:s>, <text:tab>, or <text:line-break> elements" and whose extractText returns "the text, with tabs, spaces, and newlines correctly evaluated"; odfdo's side of the same operation is Element.inner_text, "the concatenated text content of the element and its children (excluding its own tail)", with Spacer.__str__ returning `" " * self.length` where length reads text:c and falls back to one space, Tab.__str__ returning a tab and LineBreak.__str__ returning a newline, all at raw.githubusercontent.com/jdum/odfdo/v3.25.0/src/odfdo/{element,spacer,tab,line_break}.py. On generated paragraphs built out of text runs, text:s elements with and without a count, tabs and line breaks, the two libraries return the same string every time, so the expansion of the whitespace elements is a reading of the format rather than an odfpy convention. Above the paragraph they part. odfdo's Paragraph.__str__ is `self.inner_text + "\n"`, so its text of a containing element ends every paragraph, while odfpy's extractText concatenates the cells of a table with nothing between them -- exactly the join of its own per-cell extractions, which the tests assert -- and the same table therefore comes back from the two libraries as one run of characters and as a list of lines. The welded form is not invertible: two tables cut at different points, generated as head+middle, tail against head, middle+tail, produce one identical string while their cell lists differ, so nothing downstream can recover the boundary the comparison is supposed to check. The flat paragraph list conflates in both libraries alike -- odfpy's getElementsByType(P) and odfdo's body.get_paragraphs(), which is the XPath descendant::text:p, both return the body paragraphs and every cell paragraph in one list, longer than the body itself as soon as a table holds two cells -- and neither list says which entries came out of the table. One more reader disagrees with both: odfdo's Table.__str__ is a csv.writer with delimiter " " and QUOTE_NONNUMERIC over the cells' typed values, so a table whose cells carry office:string-value comes back carrying the words and a table whose cells carry only the paragraph comes back as empty quoted fields, while odfpy's extractText returns the identical text for both because it reads the paragraph and never the attribute. What this changes in P165 is the standing of "all cells in ten native tables agree exactly with the Word inputs": read cell by cell that claim is checked, and read through the table it is not, because the text of a table is a lossy join in one library, a list of lines in the second, and a rendering of attributes odfpy does not consult in the third. Which of those three a comparison sees is decided by the library the chain happens to hold, and the flat paragraph list it walks alongside them counts the cells twice over.

P162 copies slide text into native PowerPoint notes and then checks that "Twenty-six existing slide, layout, master, theme, and media XML parts remain byte-identical"; case 162 of handoff_guards_v17 types the number of parts a read adds, the note text that survives and the paragraph count that comes back. Two other implementations now answer instead. Rule 2a's search ran "node.js library extract text from ODT OpenDocument content.xml npm" and "library read pptx speaker notes independent of python-pptx node ruby java"; the second turned up the commercial Spire.Presentation for Python and Java and the converter pptx2pdfpc, and the first turned up officeparser, which reads .pptx as well as .odt. officeparser 7.8.0 was installed under node v22.22.2, because its package.json at tag v7.8.0 (raw.githubusercontent.com/harshankur/officeParser/v7.8.0/package.json) declares @xmldom/xmldom, fflate, file-type, pdfjs-dist and tesseract.js and nothing from Python, so it inflates the package and parses the XML with its own code; PHP 8.4.19's ZipArchive, which is libzip 1.22.7, lists the entries of the same package a second way. python-pptx 1.0.2's own source was read at tag v1.0.2 (raw.githubusercontent.com/scanny/python-pptx/v1.0.2/src/pptx/slide.py and src/pptx/text/text.py), where has_notes_slide is documented as the way "to test for a notes slide without the possible side effect of creating one" and notes_slide as the property where "If the slide does not have a notes slide, one is created." Executed on generated decks, that read followed by a save adds five entries to the package -- a notes slide, a notes master, the relationship part of each, and a second theme -- and it adds the same five to two decks with different titles and different numbers of paragraphs, so the cost belongs to the read and not to the deck; reading has_notes_slide instead leaves the entry list exactly as it was, and libzip agrees with zipfile about both listings. The proof's byte-identity claim is about the parts the deck already had, and it survives; what no step of the chain says is that opening a deck to look at its notes is what puts a notes slide in it. On the notes themselves the two readers agree where the text is plain. Over generated paragraphs carrying ampersands, angle brackets and quotes -- the characters the package stores as XML entities -- python-pptx and officeparser return the same strings, and python-pptx's text of the whole frame is those strings joined with the line feed that both projects document as their separator, officeparser in its README at tag v7.8.0 as a newlineDelimiter whose default is "\n". They part on a line feed inside a note. python-pptx's text.py documents both halves of the split itself: TextFrame.text assignment adds "A new paragraph ... for each line-feed character", while _Paragraph.text assignment translates each line feed "to a line-break", and the docstring names the contrast. Because the natural way to write a list of notes is to assign the first to the frame and add the rest as paragraphs, one string produces three paragraphs when it is written first and two when it is written second, and officeparser counts them the same way in both arrangements, so the list a caller passes is not the list that comes back. The break itself is where the two readers disagree: python-pptx returns it as a vertical tab, which its source explains is "how PowerPoint represents a soft carriage return in clipboard text", and officeparser returns it as the line feed that was written. What this changes in P162 is the standing of its paragraph accounting. The frame text always splits on line feeds into exactly its paragraph count, which corrects the caveat the case attaches to that identity -- no paragraph written through this library can contain a line feed of its own -- but the same notes read by the other implementation split into more lines than there are paragraphs, so "17 source paragraphs ... copied literally" is a count in python-pptx's encoding and not in the file's. A picture, meanwhile, has no text attribute at all rather than an empty one, so the unguarded shape walk the chain's first step describes raises AttributeError on the deck's own image and the guarded walk is the one that finishes.

P167 binds category amounts into a native chart and claims that "Native chart cache values and embedded Excel cells agree with the prior cost report", with a Contingency budget that "remains 0.00"; case 167 of handoff_guards_v17 types the cached values, their Python types, the cells of the embedded workbook and the result of rebinding it. No new search was needed for the second implementations: reading an xlsx is already answered here by openpyxl and by python-calamine 0.8.2, the Rust calamine binding whose pyproject.toml at tag v0.8.2 declares no dependencies, and the chart XML is read with the standard library's expat through xml.etree.ElementTree rather than with the lxml tree python-pptx itself writes, so the parser that produced the bytes is not the parser that reads them back. The element name comes from python-pptx's own ns.qn, read at tag v1.0.2 (raw.githubusercontent.com/scanny/python-pptx/v1.0.2/src/pptx/oxml/ns.py), and the chart data API in src/pptx/chart/data.py at that tag, where the number format that governs how "X and Y values are formatted in this chart and in the Excel spreadsheet" defaults to "General". Executed on generated amounts, one deck holds each amount in two places and in two forms. The cached c:v is the text of the object the caller handed in, so a Decimal of two places writes its trailing cents into the chart XML and the float of the same amount does not; the embedded workbook carries a number in both cases and never the cents. The library cannot see the difference it just wrote: chart.series[0].values returns the same floats for the Decimal deck and the float deck, so two packages that differ byte for byte read back identical through the API that made them. The workbook is read differently by its two readers as well. A whole-dollar amount reaches the sheet with no decimal point in its stored text, and openpyxl returns an int where calamine returns a float; the numbers are equal and the types are not, which is the same divergence recorded earlier for a hand-built workbook, now inside a chart's own backing sheet. A category with no figure is None in python-pptx's series and an empty cell to openpyxl, and the empty string to calamine, so "one missing budget" is a fact only two of the three readers can be asked about with `is None`. The rebinding step is where this reaches the proof's own chain, which converts the deck to ODP and back and then calls Chart.replace_data to rebuild the workbook the converter dropped. replace_data is handed the values python-pptx has just read, and those are floats. Executed on the same generated amounts, the rebuilt package holds the same numbers and not the same forms: the cents in c:v are gone, and a whole amount openpyxl read as a float out of the original sheet is an int in the rewritten one. What this changes in P167 is what "agree with the prior cost report" can mean after a round trip. The amounts agree as numbers at every stage, and the form in which they are stored does not survive: a figure written as 0.00 is 0 in the workbook and, after the rebind, 0.0 in the chart cache, and no step in the chain compares the forms, because the only reader it asks is the one that returns floats whatever is written.

P169 divides cost pools among departments by declared drivers and claims "Fifty relationship/value/rounding checks pass, including positive and negative one-cent ties, two-cent distribution, zero cost, zero weight, and exact pool conservation"; case 169 of handoff_guards_v17 types both libraries' allocations, the credit that loses a cent and the pool that stays unallocated. The two implementations were already installed and both were read at their pinned versions. largest-remainder-py 0.1.0 (raw.githubusercontent.com/fido-id/largest-remainder-py/v0.1.0/pyproject.toml and src/largest_remainder/largest_remainder.py) declares `dependencies = []`, promises "Deterministic rounding that always matches the requested total", scales the weights, floors them, and awards the shortfall to the parties whose remainders sort highest; apportionment 1.0 (raw.githubusercontent.com/martinlackner/apportionment/v1.0/setup.py and apportionment/methods.py) declares only numpy>=1.20, computes the quotas as numpy floats, truncates them, and then walks the parties in index order awarding a seat to each remainder above a cutoff and to each remainder equal to it until the pool is empty. So they share no code, and on a pool that divides the weights exactly they agree on every generated allocation, because there is no remainder to award. Where two cents have to be awarded they do not agree. Weights of a, a and 3a against a pool of 5k+3 leave all three parties a fractional quota, and the third party's fraction is the largest of the three; largest-remainder sorts and pays it, while apportionment reaches the two tied smaller remainders first, empties the pool on them, and arrives at the largest remainder with nothing left -- a case its own source records in the message "to the disadvantage of". Both allocations conserve the pool to the cent, and they are different allocations, so which department is paid the odd cent is a property of the library and not of the drivers. This is not floating point: apportionment offers fractions=True, which computes the quotas with fractions.Fraction, and on the same pools it returns exactly what its floats returned. The credit pool is worse. largest-remainder refuses a negative total outright, because "the total must be non-negative"; apportionment truncates each negative quota toward zero and then asks whether it has awarded too few, which a negative total never satisfies, so it returns without ever correcting and its allocation is short of the pool by up to one cent per party, silently. A driver of zero weight is the one place both libraries behave alike: dropping the unweighted parties from the list leaves both allocations exactly as they were, so an unweighted department neither takes a cent nor moves one. What this changes in P169 is the standing of "two-cent distribution" and of the recorded -130.00 USD credit. The chain's own guard already blocks the credit, and that block is now shown to be the only thing standing between the credit and an allocation that quietly loses cents; and the two-cent case, which the proof counts among its passing checks, is exactly the case on which the two researched implementations of the same published method return different department costs.

P171 expands leave dates into working half-day slots against a declared calendar and aggregates the days with a pandas groupby; case 171 of handoff_guards_v19 types the number of working days in September 2026, the difference between the inclusive and half-open counts, and the two employee totals. The independent implementation is workalendar 17.0.0, already used here for offsets and now handed the same generated holidays; a third view is pandas' bdate_range, which is not a third implementation and is described as what it is: its CustomBusinessDay builds an np.busdaycalendar and calls np.is_busday, read in pandas/_libs/tslibs/offsets.pyx at tag v2.2.3, so it is a second endpoint convention over numpy's own engine. numpy's counter was read at tag v2.4.6 (raw.githubusercontent.com/numpy/numpy/v2.4.6/numpy/_core/multiarray.py), where busday_count "Counts the number of valid days between `begindates` and `enddates`, not including the day of `enddates`"; workalendar's was read at tag 17.0.0 (raw.githubusercontent.com/peopledoc/workalendar/17.0.0/workalendar/core.py), where get_working_days_delta says "By default, if the day after you start is not a working day, the count will start at 0. If include_start is set to true, this day will be taken into account." Executed on generated spans and generated holiday lists, the three count three different intervals over one calendar: numpy counts [start, end), workalendar counts (start, end], and bdate_range lists [start, end], and the differences are exactly the working-day status of the endpoint each one leaves out, which is the relation the tests assert. The two implementations therefore return the same number only when the first and last day of the span have the same status, and the pair of dates a chain hands them decides whether they agree; they never disagree about which days are working days, and the generated holidays are excluded identically by both. The identity the case types as a difference of one belongs to the end date rather than to the two calls: adding a day to the end before counting returns one more than the half-open count when the last day works and returns the same number when it does not, so an inclusive leave span that ends on a Friday and one that ends on a Saturday are not one apart in the same way. The aggregation is a separate default. A timesheet row whose employee is null is dropped by pandas' groupby before it is summed, which pandas documents as its default, and the totals that come back are then short of the days that were booked; polars' group_by and a DuckDB GROUP BY both return the unattributed row as its own group, and pandas returns it too once dropna=False is passed. Nothing raises in any of them and only three of the four conserve the days. What this changes in P171 is that its recorded totals -- "Recorded usage totals 3.50 DAY" and the per-employee balances -- are conserved only while every row carries an employee, and its "Twenty-two half-day calendar slots" rest on a count whose relation to the inclusive dates in the ledger depends on the working-day status of the last date in each request, which no step of the chain records.

P187 stages cost records in DuckDB, selects "only costs through each cutoff" and computes earned-value indices as exact rationals; case 187 of handoff_guards_v20 types the two task totals, the indices and the completion estimates. Three engines now total the same generated ledgers: a DuckDB 1.5.5 DECIMAL(18,2) column, a pandas object column of decimal.Decimal and a polars 1.44.1 Decimal(18,2) column, which agree on every generated ledger including the credits, so the exactness the chain relies on is not a property of the engine it happened to use. The cutoff is where a default lives. A cost dated exactly on the cutoff is inside the reported total under `<=` and outside it under `<`, both engines agree about that in both directions, and the difference between the two totals is that record and nothing else; the proof's own step says "only costs through each cutoff" without saying which side of the boundary "through" is, and the two readings differ by exactly one record's amount on the day a chain is most likely to be asked to report. The completion estimates are where two named assumptions turn out to be one. On generated rationals, the remaining work valued at budget, ac + (bac - ev), and the budget plus the variance to date, bac + (ac - ev), return the same number every time, and z3 5.1.0 says why: asserting that the two expressions differ is unsatisfiable over the reals, so they are one formula written twice, while the third assumption, which scales the remaining work by the current efficiency, is satisfiably different and z3 produces a model. Two of the three "explicit remaining-work assumptions" the proof reports are therefore not two scenarios but one, and their agreement is not corroboration. The indices themselves keep their exactness only while they stay rational. An index whose denominator is three is not a binary fraction, so multiplying the rational by its denominator returns the earned value exactly while the float of that same index is a different number altogether -- and it is exactly the number the same chain would have got by dividing two floats, which is why nothing at the point of conversion can show that the exactness was lost. What this changes in P187 is that its exact CPI of 10/11 is exact only as long as no step converts it, that its cutoff totals depend on a comparison the chain does not declare, and that the first two of its three completion scenarios are the same scenario.

P188 validates one rooted reporting tree with networkx.is_arborescence, levels it with topological_generations, and draws the result as native PowerPoint boxes joined by bound connectors; case 188 of handoff_guards_v20 types the generation lists, one manager's descendants, the leaf list, an out-degree, four rejections and the two connector bindings. Both halves now run against second implementations. The graph oracle is igraph 1.0.0, a C library that shares no code with NetworkX and whose wheel reports the same version for its own core through igraph._igraph.__igraph_version__. NetworkX 3.6.1 was read at raw.githubusercontent.com/networkx/networkx/networkx-3.6.1/networkx/algorithms/tree/recognition.py, where is_arborescence is the single line "return is_tree(G) and max(d for n, d in G.in_degree()) <= 1" and is_tree records that for directed graphs "the underlying graph is obtained by treating each directed edge as a single undirected edge in a multigraph"; igraph's predicate was read in the C source its wheel builds, at raw.githubusercontent.com/igraph/igraph/1.0.0/src/properties/trees.c, which states that "In the directed case, an additional requirement is that all edges are oriented away from a root (out-tree or arborescence) or all edges are oriented towards a root (in-tree or anti-arborescence)", and the mode argument of the Python binding at raw.githubusercontent.com/igraph/python-igraph/1.0.0/src/_igraph/graphobject.c. On generated rooted structures of up to twelve positions the two agree on every verdict, and both flip together when one position is given a second manager, so the rejection case 188 typed by hand is now the rejection of two libraries. The levels agree as well: the index of the generation topological_generations puts a position in is exactly igraph's distance from the root, computed by a different algorithm, on every generated tree. Three divergences follow. The first is the empty organisation. NetworkX's is_tree raises NetworkXPointlessConcept before is_arborescence can answer, so a reporting structure with no positions leaves the validator by a different exception class from the one a malformed structure raises, while igraph answers, and its C source says why: "By convention, the null graph (i.e. the graph with no vertices) is considered not to be connected, and therefore not a tree." The second is the repeated reporting line. DiGraph holds at most one edge per ordered pair, so a file that declares the same manager-to-report line twice is the same graph as one that declares it once and passes is_arborescence unchanged, while igraph keeps both declarations as parallel edges and rejects the structure, the two edge counts differing by exactly the repetition. Which reading is right is a question about the source file rather than about trees, and P188's validator cannot ask it. The third is the level itself. topological_generations layers a graph by removing the positions with no manager and repeating, so a position's level is the longest chain of reporting lines that reaches it and not its distance from the top, and the two coincide only while the structure is a tree. On a chain of positions carrying one extra line from the root to the last of them, still acyclic and recognised as such by both libraries, the level and the distance part company, and a chart drawn from the levels puts a position that reports to the chief executive at the bottom of the page. python-igraph 1.0.0 exposes no is_forest, although the C library it wraps documents igraph_is_forest at the same tag, so the two-roots half of case 188 is corroborated by connectivity instead: both libraries agree that the union of two rooted structures is acyclic and not weakly connected, and NetworkX's own is_forest returns the opposite verdict to its is_arborescence on that graph. The deck half needed a second reader of the OOXML package, and the search under rule 2a found one outside Python. LibreOffice 24.2.7.2 is installed on this machine but cannot serve: its Impress and Writer filters are absent, and soffice --convert-to answers "Error: source file could not be loaded" for a .pptx and for a plain text file alike. The oracle is Apache POI 5.4.1 under OpenJDK 21.0.10, a Java implementation of the same package format, whose dependency list was read at repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/apache/poi/poi-ooxml/5.4.1/poi-ooxml-5.4.1.pom and repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/apache/poi/poi/5.4.1/poi-5.4.1.pom: poi, poi-ooxml-lite, xmlbeans, commons-compress, commons-io, commons-codec, commons-collections4, commons-math3, curvesapi, SparseBitSet and log4j-api, with nothing from Python among them. Its accessors were read at raw.githubusercontent.com/apache/poi/REL_5_4_1/poi-ooxml/src/main/java/org/apache/poi/xslf/usermodel/XSLFShape.java and the XSLFSimpleShape.java beside it: getShapeId, getShapeName, the "public final XmlObject getXmlObject()" documented as "the xml bean holding this shape's data", and getAnchor, which converts the stored offsets with Units.toPoints. python-pptx 1.0.2's own connector code was read at raw.githubusercontent.com/scanny/python-pptx/v1.0.2/src/pptx/shapes/connector.py. Three readers then agree on what a bound connector says: for every generated reporting tree the shape ids and connection indices POI reads out of the saved package are the ids python-pptx reported when it wrote them and the ones the standard library's expat parser finds in the slide XML, and POI's anchors in points are python-pptx's own lengths through Length.pt. The claim that the connectors preserve their exact parent and child shape ids therefore holds under an independent reader rather than under a regular expression over the writing library's own XML, which is what the guard used, because python-pptx offers no way to read a binding back: begin_connect and end_connect write, and nothing reads. Two findings came with that. begin_connect is "self._connect_begin_to(shape, cxn_pt_idx)" followed by "self._move_begin_to_cxn(shape, cxn_pt_idx)", and the second of those is a dictionary of four entries subscripted by the index, so a fifth connection point raises KeyError after the stCxn element is already in the tree: the deck still saves, the connector keeps whatever geometry it had, and POI reads back a connector bound to a connection point the library that wrote it cannot place. That method's own docstring warns only that such an index "could lead to a load error if cxn_pt_idx exceeds the connection point count available on the connected shape", and marks the whole method EXPERIMENTAL. The other finding is that a binding is a reference plus a copy: connecting copies the shape's connection point into the connector once, so moving the shape afterwards leaves the connector where it was while the id in the file still names the moved shape. P188's own sentence that "Desktop dragging and connector rerouting behavior remain unverified" is exact, and this is its other half -- the file as written already disagrees with itself the moment a position moves, and only an application that re-routes on open reconciles the two.

P180 detects conflicting bookings with pandas.Interval.overlaps and pandas.IntervalIndex.overlaps under a start-inclusive, end-exclusive contract; case 180 of handoff_guards_v19 types fourteen verdicts about which bookings touch. Two independent implementations of the same relation now answer the same questions. The first is portion 2.6.2, whose pyproject.toml at tag 2.6.2 declares "sortedcontainers~=2.4" and nothing else, so none of pandas is under it, and whose overlaps and adjacent were read at raw.githubusercontent.com/AlexandreDecan/portion/2.6.2/portion/interval.py. The second is Guava 33.7.1-jre under OpenJDK 21.0.10, reached through a shim: its dependency list at repo1.maven.org/maven2/com/google/guava/guava/33.7.1-jre/guava-33.7.1-jre.pom is failureaccess, listenablefuture, jspecify, error_prone_annotations and j2objc-annotations, and its Range was read at raw.githubusercontent.com/google/guava/v33.7.1/guava/src/com/google/common/collect/Range.java. pandas' own rule was read at raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/v2.2.3/pandas/_libs/interval.pyx, where overlaps is documented as "Two intervals overlap if they share a common point, including closed endpoints. Intervals that only have an open endpoint in common do not overlap." On generated bookings under every combination of the four closures the three libraries return the same verdict, so the closure contradiction case 180 recorded is reproduced rather than resolved: the same four timestamps conflict under closed-on-both-ends and do not conflict under the start-inclusive reading, in all three. What the second and third implementations add is a distinction pandas does not make. A booking that starts exactly when another ends and a booking that starts hours later are one answer from overlaps and two answers from the others: portion calls the first pair adjacent, "if they do not overlap and their union form a single atomic interval", and Guava calls it connected, its own documentation giving this very case -- "[2, 4) and [4, 6) are connected, because both enclose the empty range [4, 4)". P180's chain classifies coverage gaps, and a handover and an empty hour are the same value in the only predicate it uses. Two further findings concern what a booking is. Comparing a booking closed on the right with one closed on the left raises nothing in any of the three, and the shared endpoint belongs to both, so records whose closures were set in different places conflict where the same clock times under one closure do not, with nothing in the answer to show that two rules were mixed. And a booking of no length exists in three different senses: pandas builds the Interval for all four closures and reports the closure back, and it conflicts with itself under exactly one of them; portion collapses three of the four to the empty interval, so the closure is no longer recoverable from the value; Guava refuses the fourth outright, its open factory documented to throw IllegalArgumentException "if lower is greater than or equal to upper", which reaches the tests as a non-zero exit. The last of the four typed claims is the index. IntervalIndex.overlaps compares the probe with every interval in the index, the probe included when it is one of them, and the vector it returns agrees with portion booking by booking; the extra hit is exactly the probe's verdict on itself, which is not always a hit, because a zero-length booking closed at neither end does not overlap itself. The drop_self correction the chain applies is therefore right for every booking that lasts and wrong for one that does not.

P194 is one of the ten proofs this file records as a theoretical requirement, so neither its positive test nor its three adverse tests had ever been run against anything but pySHACL; case 194 of handoff_guards_v21 executed them there and typed the four verdicts. They now run against a second implementation of the same W3C recommendation, rdf-validate-shacl 0.6.5 under node v22.22.2, whose package.json at tag v0.6.5 declares @rdfjs/data-model, @rdfjs/dataset, @rdfjs/environment, @rdfjs/namespace, @rdfjs/term-set, @vocabulary/sh, clownface, debug, rdf-dataset-ext, rdf-literal and rdf-validate-datatype, an RDF/JS stack with nothing from Python in it, and whose README at that tag calls it "An implementation of the W3C SHACL specification on top of the RDFJS stack". pySHACL 0.40.1's entry point was read at raw.githubusercontent.com/RDFLib/pySHACL/v0.40.1/pyshacl/entrypoints.py, where validate takes the advanced flag the chain passes and returns the conformance flag, the report graph and its text. The shapes graph and every data graph here are built with rdflib 7.6.0's own vocabulary objects and handed to the second implementation as turtle written by rdflib's serializer, so no turtle is authored. The two implementations agree on all four of P194's named cases over generated control identifiers, owners, dates and class names. A control with an owner and a typed evidence date conforms with no results in both. Removing the owner link is exactly one violation in both. A literal carrying the date datatype with no date in it is exactly one violation in both, although one library reaches that verdict through rdflib's lexical parser and the other through rdf-validate-datatype. And a node whose class is not the targeted one conforms, with a report identical to the report for a graph that satisfies every constraint. That last agreement is the finding. The vacuous pass is not one library's default; it is what the recommendation requires. w3.org is blocked from this environment, so the specification was read in its own source repository, github.com/w3c/data-shapes at commit 9c863967bceaef1a87c24e4dd761eda763823120, in shacl/index.html: "The value of sh:conforms is true if and only if the validation did not produce any validation results, and false otherwise." A shape reaches nodes only through its target declarations, so a node no target selects produces no results, and no results is conformance. P194's own contract already says "Zero targeted nodes cannot count as success when controls were expected", and the executed pair shows why that sentence has to be enforced outside the validator: for a graph whose controls carry the wrong class, two independent implementations return the report of a conforming graph. An empty data graph conforms in both as well, so a validation report alone cannot tell a complete inventory from an empty file. What does tell them apart is the reconciliation the proof requires beside the shapes: rdflib's own subjects() lists the nodes carrying the targeted class, the expected identifiers absent from that list are the coverage defect, and a DuckDB EXCEPT over the same two lists finds the same ones. The three adverse mutations P194 names are therefore executed rather than theoretical, and the third of them is caught by nothing inside SHACL.

P198 is another of the proofs recorded as a theoretical requirement. It asks a solver for a point of the declared domain that no decision row covers, and for a point that more than one row answers; case 198 of handoff_guards_v21 ran those queries in z3 and typed the witnesses. They now run in two solvers, z3 5.1.0 and cvc5 1.3.4, whose decision procedures share no code and whose wheels declare no dependency on each other, with the rows built by applying the standard library's operator functions to each solver's own integer variable so that neither table is written twice. On generated thresholds and domain floors the two agree throughout. Rows below and at-or-above one threshold make both the gap query and the overlap query unsatisfiable, which is P198's theoretical positive test executed. Moving the second row from at-or-above to strictly above the threshold makes the gap query satisfiable in both, and both return the same witness, the threshold itself, from any floor at or below it. A second row admitting everything from a lower threshold makes the overlap query satisfiable in both, and each solver's own model evaluates the conjunction of the rows to true, so the witness is checked by the solver that produced it. Raising the floor above the threshold removes the gap in both, which is the contract sentence "Totality is relative to the declared domain" made executable: the same table is total or not according to a bound that is not in the table. One divergence appeared, and it is in the plumbing rather than in the logic. A decision table with a single row is a coverage question in z3 and an error in cvc5. z3's Or, read at raw.githubusercontent.com/Z3Prover/z3/z3-5.1.0/src/api/python/z3/z3.py, passes whatever it is given to Z3_mk_or, which accepts one argument, so Or([p]) is p. cvc5's pythonic Or, read at raw.githubusercontent.com/cvc5/cvc5_pythonic_api/726058d8f23968883d819d81843f48acd13d40f9/cvc5_pythonic_api/cvc5_pythonic.py, collapses a single expression but not a single-element list -- its guard is "if len(args) == 1 and type(args[0]) is not list: return args[0]" -- and its term manager then refuses the kind, with "invalid kind 'OR', expected Terms with kind OR must have at least 2 children". The same holds for And, so both of P198's queries are affected. Declaring the identical row twice is accepted by both and returns z3's answer, which establishes that the refusal is about the length of the list and not about the question. P198's helper builds its query from a list comprehension over the rows, and case 198 itself asks a one-row question, so this is on the path the proof describes: under one solver the coverage claim is answered, and under the other it raises RuntimeError before any decision procedure runs. The finite enumeration the proof keeps beside the solver was checked as well: itertools.product over a range is the grid numpy's indices produces for the same shape, in the same order and with the same number of points.

P177 states the identity of a manifest row as a pandera schema, with unique=['movement', 'package'] and a membership check on the declared movements; case 177 of handoff_guards_v19 types the accepted row count, six rejections and the index of a concatenated frame. Two engines that do not share pandas' data model now answer the same questions: polars 1.44.1, whose is_duplicated and is_in run over frames that have no index at all, and DuckDB 1.5.5, told the same contract as a primary key over the pair and a foreign key into the declared movements. On generated manifests of distinct rows all three agree: pandera returns the frame unchanged, polars counts as many unique rows as it has rows, and DuckDB keeps every row. On a manifest that declares one of its rows twice all three reject, and they name the same row: pandera reports multiple_fields_uniqueness, polars flags both copies and nothing else, DuckDB refuses the insert on the primary key. On a row naming a movement outside the declared set the same holds, with pandera's failure_cases carrying exactly the movement polars and the foreign key single out. The divergence is the index, and it is the finding case 177 was pointing at. pandas.concat keeps the index label of every row it appends, so appending a row that is already in the frame produces a frame carrying that label twice, and pandera's uniqueness report then fails while it is formatting the failure it found. Its check_column_values_are_unique, read at raw.githubusercontent.com/unionai-oss/pandera/v0.33.1/pandera/backends/pandas/container.py, calls check_obj.duplicated to find the repeated rows and then hands them to reshape_failure_cases, which at raw.githubusercontent.com/unionai-oss/pandera/v0.33.1/pandera/backends/pandas/error_formatters.py is failure_cases.unstack().reset_index(); pandas refuses to reshape a frame whose index repeats a label and raises ValueError("Columns with duplicate values are not supported in stack"). A caller that catches pandera's SchemaErrors does not catch that, so the manifest is neither accepted nor rejected: the validator that was supposed to decide raises an exception of a class the chain does not handle. Resetting the index first turns the identical data into an ordinary rejection, which is what the chain's reset_index flag is doing and what case 177 recorded without saying why. Neither other engine has the failure mode to begin with, and polars returns the same duplication verdict for the concatenated frame and for the reset one, because the label pandas is reshaping on is not part of the data in the first place.

P199 is the gate itself: a bound artifact hash, a state, a role and a date decide whether a control is satisfied, and case 199 of handoff_guards_v21 types the satisfied verdict and each of its four blocked reasons. Three of the four are now executed against second implementations, and each of the three rests on a text comparison the libraries under it do not require. The hash first. hashlib.sha256 here is _hashlib.openssl_sha256, so the digest the chain computes is OpenSSL's; neither oracle is. PHP 8.4.19 carries its own SHA-256 in ext/hash, read at raw.githubusercontent.com/php/php-src/php-8.4.19/ext/hash/hash_sha.c, and Ruby 3.3.6 vendors Aaron D. Gifford's implementation, read at raw.githubusercontent.com/ruby/ruby/v3_3_6/ext/digest/sha2/sha2.h, which Digest::SHA256.ancestors confirms is the class in use here rather than OpenSSL::Digest. Over generated artifacts the three agree on every digest, which is what makes the two findings that follow properties of the binding and not of one library. The first is the case of the text. CPython documents hexdigest at raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.11.15/Doc/library/hashlib.rst as returning "a string object of double length, containing only hexadecimal digits" and says nothing about which case; PHP documents hash in php/doc-en at reference/hash/functions/hash.xml as returning "the calculated message digest as lowercase hexits"; Ruby writes lowercase as well. The three converge on a convention the format does not impose, and the gate compares the declared digest with the computed one as text, so a declaration transcribed in capitals is refused although it is the same number: bytes.fromhex reads it back to the bytes all three runtimes computed. hmac.compare_digest refuses it too, and that is the callable CPython publishes for this exact comparison, documented in Doc/library/hmac.rst at the same tag as returning "a == b" through "an approach designed to prevent timing analysis by avoiding content-based short circuiting behaviour". The blocked reason 'artifact does not match the bound hash' therefore covers a correct declaration written in the other case. The second finding is what the digest binds at all. Composed and decomposed spellings of one accented string are the same text to unicodedata and to polars' str.normalize, whose docstring at raw.githubusercontent.com/pola-rs/polars/py-1.44.1/py-polars/src/polars/series/string.py says it "Returns the Unicode normal form of the string values" using "the forms described in Unicode Standard Annex 15" and does it in Rust rather than through CPython's tables; their digests are two different numbers. Evidence re-saved by an editor that normalizes fails the artifact clause while reading identically to every party to the approval, and nothing in the chain records which normalization the bound bytes were in. The resolution step is next. P199 binds each case to its approval with merge(validate='one_to_one'), documented at raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/v2.2.3/pandas/core/frame.py as "one_to_one" or "1:1": check if merge keys are unique in both left and right datasets, and polars 1.44.1 documents the same check at py-polars/src/polars/dataframe/frame.py as "One-to-one. Checks if join keys are unique in both left and right datasets." Executed over generated cases and approvals the two agree on both sides: each refuses a repeated case and each refuses a repeated approval, with MergeError and ComputeError. What neither checks is coverage. A control case with no approval row at all is not a cardinality failure in pandas, in polars or in DuckDB; the inner join drops it, so it reaches no gate, receives no blocked reason and appears in no exception routing, and the chain's actionable exception for an unapproved control is an absent row. It is recoverable only outside the check, from the outer join's indicator, the column pandas documents as taking "left_only" for observations whose merge key only appears in the left DataFrame, or from a set difference in SQL, and both name exactly the cases the validated join discarded. The asymmetry runs the other way too: a case declared twice under a key no approval names cannot change what the join returns, and both engines still refuse the merge, so the guard fires on rows the gate would never have seen and stays silent about the case the gate never sees. The time clause is the third. The gate compares the approval date with the evaluation time as text. On the zero-padded ISO form that is the calendar ordering, and three implementations say so over generated pairs: CPython's date comparison, the Julian day number Ruby's Date#jd returns, documented in ext/date/date_core.c at tag v3_3_6 as "Returns the Julian day number", and the Unix timestamp PHP's DateTimeImmutable::getTimestamp returns, documented in php/doc-en at reference/datetime/datetimeinterface/gettimestamp.xml as "Gets the Unix timestamp". Two generated regions break it. An approval written without the leading zero on a one-digit month sorts after the evaluation date as text and before it as a date; Ruby's Date.parse, which its own documentation calls a method that "recognizes many forms in +string+, but it is not a validator", and PHP's DateTimeImmutable both read it as the same calendar day CPython does and both order it earlier, so the gate returns 'blocked: approval post-dates the evaluation time' for an approval that precedes it. And an approval carrying a clock time on the evaluation day is longer than the date it falls on and therefore greater as text at every hour of that day including midnight, while both runtimes read it as that same day. The validation step the chain declares does not close either gap, because it and the comparison exclude each other. pydantic 2.13.5's TypeAdapter for datetime.date returns a datetime.date for the padded record, and comparing that value with the evaluation text is a TypeError and not a decision; the unpadded record it refuses outright; and the same-day stamp it refuses at every second but one, following the rule it documents at raw.githubusercontent.com/pydantic/pydantic/v2.13.5/docs/api/standard_library_types.md, "If the validation fails, the input can be validated as a datetime (including as numbers), provided that the time component is 0 and that it is naive." Executed, the second condition in that sentence does not hold: a midnight stamp carrying any offset from minus fourteen to plus fourteen hours is accepted and validates to the local calendar date it was written with, the offset discarded, while the same instant written in UTC, the same instant by PHP's count to the second, is refused as date_from_datetime_inexact. So which day an approval is dated to is the offset its recorder happened to use, and two spellings of one moment reach the gate as one date and one refusal. The field is either validated, and then not comparable, or comparable, and then unvalidated, and P199's chain names both steps.

P172 and P174 are two membership questions from the same v19 batch, and both turn on a default nobody passed. P172 declares a window that is start-inclusive and end-exclusive and builds it with pandas.date_range, whose parameter is documented at raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/v2.2.3/pandas/core/indexes/datetimes.py as "inclusive : {"both", "neither", "left", "right"}, default "both"". polars 1.44.1 carries the same default, "closed: ClosedInterval = "both"" in py-polars/src/polars/functions/range/date_range.py at tag py-1.44.1, and DuckDB 1.5.5 ships both readings under two names: its documentation, read in the duckdb-web checkout at commit 6f6cd1659f0e2ddd1965b1d3f1833e7fc512e7ac in docs/current/sql/functions/list.md, says of range "The start parameter is inclusive, while the stop parameter is exclusive." and of generate_series "Both the start and the stop parameters are inclusive.", and introduces the pair with "The two functions' behavior is different regarding their stop argument." Over generated spans the three agree closure by closure. The default day list is the same in all three and contains the end date the chain declares excluded; the left-closed list is the same in all three; and the default list is the left-closed list with that one date appended, which is the whole of the difference. The four closures pandas and polars both offer are six pairwise different day lists, so the window is entirely the argument passed and the reading the chain declares is not the one it gets by saying nothing. The second membership primitive of the same chain closes the other end. pandas.Interval is documented in pandas/_libs/interval.pyx at the same tag as "closed : {'right', 'left', 'both', 'neither'}, default 'right'", so over the same two bounds the default day list contains the start date and the default interval does not, and portion 2.6.2 returns the same two answers for that closure, which places the exclusion in the closure and not in pandas. Under the declared closure the two intervals disagree about both endpoints and agree about every day strictly between them. P174 is the other half: an unknown shortfall must stay unknown rather than become a zero request, and what the libraries do with it depends on the dtype the frame happens to carry. pandas' own missing-data guide at doc/source/user_guide/missing_data.rst at tag v2.2.3 states the split, "In equality and comparison operations, :class:`NA` also propagates. This deviates from the behaviour of ``np.nan``, where comparisons with ``np.nan`` always return ``False``." Executed on generated line lists carrying exactly one unknown quantity, the float64 column answers False for the unknown line and so names nothing, while the nullable Int64 column, polars and DuckDB all answer unknown and name the same line; DuckDB documents its rule in docs/current/sql/data_types/nulls.md at the same commit as "Any comparison with a NULL value returns NULL, including NULL = NULL." Two consequences follow and they point opposite ways. Every engine totals the column identically: pandas in both dtypes, polars and DuckDB all skip the missing value, so the unknown line contributes zero to any sum, which is precisely the state the contract says must not arise. And the selection that separates requested lines from the rest covers every line in one reading and loses one in three. Negating the same comparison keeps the unknown line in the float64 frame, where it sits beside a line whose shortfall is a real zero and is indistinguishable from it, and drops it in the nullable frame, in polars and in DuckDB, where the negation of unknown is unknown and unknown is not true. So in three of the four readings the unknown line is in neither the requested set nor its complement: the two queries a reader would write to cover every line cover every line but that one, and nothing reports it. Only an explicit null test finds it, and all four readings agree about which line that is.

P195 measures a clause before and after Unicode normalization and reports what moved, and case 195 of handoff_guards_v21 types the four counts and the four change kinds. The counts now come from three implementations of NFC that share no code: CPython's unicodedata, polars 1.44.1's str.normalize, which is the Rust unicode-normalization crate declared in crates/polars-ops/Cargo.toml at tag py-1.44.1 and documented in py-polars/src/polars/series/string.py at that tag as returning "the Unicode normal form of the string values" using "the forms described in Unicode Standard Annex 15", and Ruby 3.3.6's String#unicode_normalize, which is written in Ruby rather than bound to ICU: raw.githubusercontent.com/ruby/ruby/v3_3_6/lib/unicode_normalize/normalize.rb, by Ayumu Nojima and Martin J. Durst, records that it and its generated tables "are part of the implementation of the built-in String class, not part of the standard library". Over generated accented text the three agree on the composed form, on its length in characters and on its length in bytes, and each of those counts differs from the count taken in the text the offsets were recorded against. The consequence is executed rather than argued: the last offset that indexes the raw clause is past the end of the normalized one, where the primitive raises IndexError instead of returning a character, and below that the two spellings do not agree character by character either, so an offset that is still in range selects something else. The reverse claim is executed too. The composed and decomposed spellings are two different strings to polars' comparison and one string once either is normalized, in all three implementations, so an equality check run after normalizing reports no change to a clause whose recorded bytes did change, and that is the check a chain would use to look for exactly that change. Normalizing twice is normalizing once in all three, so the loss runs one way only. And which normal form the chain names is itself a decision: on an alphabet built out of the Unicode database, every character of which carries a compatibility decomposition, is its own canonical form and is not its own compatibility form, NFC changes nothing and NFKC changes every character, in all three implementations, so a chain that says only "normalization" has not said whether the recorded clause survives. The second half of case 195 reports what kind of change was made between two versions of a clause and reads the kinds off difflib's opcodes; rapidfuzz 3.14.6's own edit script is the second implementation. Where the clause has no repeated character and the edit introduces one that is not in it, the two agree on insertion, deletion, replacement and no change over generated bases and positions. Where the clause repeats they do not, and difflib says as much about itself: its documentation at raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.11.15/Doc/library/difflib.rst describes the algorithm as recursively finding "the longest contiguous matching subsequence" and warns that "This does not yield minimal edit sequences, but does tend to yield matches that "look right" to people." Executed on a generated repeating run with one character replaced in its first half, rapidfuzz returns one operation, which is the edit distance it also reports, and difflib returns an insertion and a deletion where one substitution was made. Worse for a version report, the same differ answers the same edit two ways according to how long the surrounding text is. difflib documents the reason at the same tag: "If an item's duplicates (after the first one) account for more than 1% of the sequence and the sequence is at least 200 items long, this item is marked as "popular" and is treated as junk for the purpose of sequence matching. This heuristic can be turned off by setting the ``autojunk`` argument to ``False``". Once the generated run passes two hundred characters that heuristic is on, difflib agrees with rapidfuzz that one substitution was made, and disagrees with itself run with autojunk off, which returns what it returned for the shorter run. So the kind of change P195 reports is a function of which differ ran and of the length of the document it ran on, and P195 records neither beside the finding.

P181 renders authored passages into a page and reads them back with lxml's HTML parser, and case 181 of handoff_guards_v20 types the recovered text, the element counts and the parser refusal. The second implementation of HTML parsing is html5lib 1.1, which its README at tag 1.1 calls "a pure-python library for parsing HTML" that "is designed to conform to the WHATWG HTML specification, as is implemented by all major web browsers", and whose setup.py at that tag declares six and webencodings; lxml appears there only as an optional extra, and the etree treebuilder these tests ask for does not reach it, so what is being compared is libxml2's C parser against a pure-Python implementation of the WHATWG algorithm. The two agree everywhere, which is what makes each finding a property of HTML rather than of one reader. On a page rendered with jinja2's escaping on, both return every generated passage exactly as it was written. On the same passages rendered with escaping off, which is jinja2 3.1.6's default as the P151 tests above already record, both still return every passage exactly as written, so a check that reads the page back and compares finds nothing wrong, while both XML parsers refuse the very same bytes, lxml with XMLSyntaxError and the standard library's expat binding with ParseError. The characters that region is generated from were read off those two parsers at import rather than named here: of the five printable characters jinja2's escaping changes, exactly two make both XML parsers refuse the page. A passage that itself contains markup is not refused by either HTML parser and does not change the shape of the page: the tags are dropped, the text between them is kept, and the page has as many rows as the escaped page does, so the one quantity a chain counting rows would notice is the one that does not move, while the text it reads back is not the text it rendered. A passage that contains a closing tag becomes two rows in both parsers, split in the same place, where escaping the same passage returns one row holding the text as written; the number of rows a reader sees is therefore decided by a flag on the renderer and not by the number of passages. And the identifier that would bind a row back to the passage it came from is on only one of the two. Both parsers report an id for the first row and nothing for the second, and dropping the rows that have no id leaves exactly the identifiers the escaped page has, so the page carries one identifier and two rows and a reader keyed on the identifier cannot see the second row at all.

The glue-elimination module is itself a set of claims, and this is the first of them to be executed against second implementations. handoff_guards_v18 replaced two hand-written bill-of-materials traversals with scipy.sparse.linalg.spsolve on the Leontief total-requirements system and typed the six cables a kit needs. Two further engines now answer the same question over generated acyclic bills: numpy.linalg.solve, which is LAPACK through a dense factorisation rather than SuperLU through a sparse one, and a DuckDB recursive expansion, which multiplies quantities along every path and adds them up without solving anything. The three agree on the totals and on their linearity in the demand. They do not agree in the same way, though: the expansion is exact, and the two solvers agree only inside the forward-error bound numpy itself computes, machine epsilon times the condition number of the system times the size of the answer, because a direct solver's answer for a part the demand does not reach is small rather than zero. Asking whether an entry is non-zero is therefore not the same as asking whether the part is required, and only the expansion, which never mentions the parts it does not reach, answers the second question exactly. The refusal case is the finding. v18's chain tests acyclicity with NetworkX before it solves, and that test is doing all of the refusing. Handed a generated bill whose parts require each other around a loop, neither solver raises and neither warns: both return the same finite vector, and its smallest entry is negative, which is not a quantity of anything. The recursive expansion is the only one of the three that cannot be asked at all, because on those bills it does not terminate, and the tests do not ask it. And when each part in the loop takes exactly one of the next, so that the matrix is exactly singular, the two solvers part company. numpy documents "If `a` is singular or not square." as the condition for LinAlgError in numpy/linalg/_linalg.py at tag v2.4.6, and raises it. scipy warns and returns instead: MatrixRankWarning is exported from scipy/sparse/linalg/_dsolve/linsolve.py at tag v1.17.1 and documented there as "Warning for exactly singular matrices.", and the same file's spsolve warns "Matrix is exactly singular" and then calls x.fill(np.nan). A chain that catches solver exceptions sees nothing at all on the sparse path, and the answer it carries forward is a vector with no finite entry in it.

The other fresh claim in the glue-elimination module is that a deterministic package is a library writer, and case a_deterministic_package_is_a_library_writer of handoff_guards_v18 types the digest equality, the 1980-01-01 stamp and the standard library's clock. The primitive is repro-zipfile 0.4.1, read at its own tag before use: raw.githubusercontent.com/drivendataorg/repro-zipfile/v0.4.1/repro_zipfile/__init__.py, where ReproducibleZipFile is documented as a replacement for zipfile.ZipFile that "overwrites file-modified timestamps and file/directory permissions modes in write mode in order to create a reproducible ZIP archive", and where the published date_time() is the value "used to force overwrite on all ZipInfo objects. Defaults to 1980-01-01 00:00:00." Its README at the same tag states the claim the chains rest on, verbatim: ""Reproducible" or "deterministic" in this context means that the binary content of the ZIP archive is identical if you add files with identical binary content in the same order. It means you can reliably check equality of the contents of two ZIP archives by simply comparing checksums of the archive using a hash function like MD5 or SHA-256." Rule 2a's search found three implementations of the format that share no code with it and depend on nothing from Python: java.util.zip in the OpenJDK class library, libzip 1.7.3 behind PHP's zip extension, and Go's archive/zip. The first two are used here, both as readers and as writers; the third was recorded and not used, because two implementations already answer every claim in this cluster and a third would add a runtime to the reference list without moving any finding. Both were read at their pinned versions: OpenJDK 21.0.10 at raw.githubusercontent.com/openjdk/jdk21u/jdk-21.0.10-ga/src/java.base/share/classes/java/util/zip/, and libzip at raw.githubusercontent.com/nih-at/libzip/v1.7.3/lib/zip_dirent.c, reached from PHP through the statIndex macro at raw.githubusercontent.com/php/php-src/php-8.4.19/ext/zip/php_zip.c, which copies libzip's own mtime field out unchanged. Four of the case's claims survive contact with them.
