Two packages written from the same generated parts in the same order are one digest; every part comes back out under the name and at the length it went in with, in both runtimes; the entry stamp another runtime reads out of the MS-DOS date and time fields, through ZipEntry.getTimeLocal, is exactly the date-time the library publishes; and the standard library writer stamps the clock where the replacement stamps the constant, which is the reason the package exists and which its README gives as "ZIP archives are not normally reproducible even when containing files with identical content because of file metadata. In particular, the usual culprits are: 1. Last-modified timestamps". What does not survive is the reading the chains take from that: that the digest of the package stands for its content. Handed the same parts, the java.util.zip writer produces the same names in the same order carrying the same bytes with the same MS-DOS local date-times, stored uncompressed as these are, and a different archive: different length, different digest, and the difference is framing rather than content. The package's own README says the order matters, verbatim "Note that files must be written to the archive in the same order to reproduce an identical archive", and that is executed here too, on generated permutations that leave the mapping of name to bytes identical and the digest different. So a package digest identifies content, order and writer together, and two builds of the same parts match only if the same writer built both. The stamp itself is smaller than the chains treat it as being, in three separate ways. The MS-DOS time field stores seconds in units of two, which libzip's reader spells out as `tm.tm_sec = (dtime << 1) & 62`, so an odd SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH cannot be written down: date_time() goes on reporting the odd second while the archive carries the even one, and two epochs a second apart produce one archive byte for byte. The floor is unguarded in the other direction. The Reproducible Builds standard the README points at puts no lower bound on SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, and the format does; CPython guards it, raising ValueError('ZIP does not support timestamps before 1980') in ZipInfo.__init__ at raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.11.15/Lib/zipfile.py, but the replacement writer assigns zinfo.date_time after the ZipInfo is constructed, so that guard never runs and the write dies inside struct.pack instead, with a struct.error about an unsigned short. And the fixed value the README calls "1980-01-01 00:00 UTC" is not stored as UTC or as anything else: the field carries no zone, and libzip resolves it with the reader's, filling a struct tm and returning mktime(&tm) under the comment "let mktime decide if DST is in effect". Run in a generated zone, PHP dates the same package to the instant zoneinfo gives for that calendar reading read as local time there, which is a different instant from the UTC one by the zone's offset. The stamp is stable across machines as a calendar reading and not as an instant, so any chain that turns it into one -- a retention window, an age check, an ordering against a wall-clock event -- gets a different answer on a differently configured machine. The last finding is about the one date the README names. OpenJDK's ZipEntry encodes 1980-01-01 00:00:00 as `(1 << 21) | (1 << 16)`, which is the same bit pattern the same file keeps as its sentinel `DOSTIME_BEFORE_1980`; setTimeLocal tests `xdostime != DOSTIME_BEFORE_1980` before it discards the modification time, so at exactly this stamp it keeps one instead, converted through ZoneId.systemDefault(), and ZipOutputStream then writes an Info-ZIP extended timestamp extra field holding that instant, against its own comment "by default, do NOT use extended timestamps in extra data, for now." Executed, the second writer produces two different archives for the same parts in two zones at that stamp, and one archive in both zones at every later even second the tests generate, up to 2038. The earliest timestamp the format admits, chosen for reproducibility, is the single point in the format's range at which this writer is not reproducible.

The last of that module's fresh claims is that month ends come from periods and not from repeated addition, and its case month_ends_come_from_periods_not_from_repeated_addition types the three ends, the period text and the days in February. The primitives are pandas 2.2.3's period_range, Period.end_time and Period.days_in_month, read at the pinned tag: end_time is documented in pandas/_libs/tslibs/period.pyx at raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/v2.2.3/pandas/_libs/tslibs/period.pyx as "Get the Timestamp for the end of the period." Three implementations that share none of that code agree with it on generated dates across two centuries. polars 1.44.1's dt.month_end, documented at raw.githubusercontent.com/pola-rs/polars/py-1.44.1/py-polars/src/polars/expr/datetime.py as "Roll forward to the last day of the month.", and DuckDB 1.5.5's last_day, documented in the duckdb-web checkout at commit 6f6cd1659f0e2ddd1965b1d3f1833e7fc512e7ac (docs/current/sql/functions/date.md) as "The last day of the corresponding month in the date.", give the same date as pandas for every generated anchor, leap Februaries included; PHP 8.4.19's relative format "last day of", handled by timelib in C in another runtime, gives it a fourth time; and the days in the month agree with CPython's own calendar.monthrange, which is pure Python and unrelated to pandas' C extension. The month end is a property of the calendar, which is what makes the drift a defect rather than a convention. That drift is reproduced exactly, on generated years and on the months the calendar module itself reports as longer than the month after them. From the end of such a month one relativedelta(months=+1) lands on the next month end, because clamping and the month end are the same date there, and the second step carries the shortened day forward and never recovers it: a three-month walk from 31 January ends on 28 March where the period range ends on the 31st, which is the value v16 recorded and v18 typed. One hop of two months from the same anchor is right, so what is broken is stepping repeatedly rather than the offset. A monthly period cannot drift for a reason worth stating: it carries no day at all. Any other day of the same month gives the same period, the same text and the same end, which is executed here on a day drawn from the length the calendar module reports for that month. Two of the case's other claims are smaller than they look. end_time is not a date but the last instant of the period: the gap between it and the next period's start is exactly Timestamp.resolution, one nanosecond, so a deadline compared as a date admits nothing after midnight while the same deadline compared against the period's own end admits the whole of the last day, and the .date() the chain takes discards that silently. And the word for monthly is not one word. to_offset in pandas/_libs/tslibs/offsets.pyx at tag v2.2.3 warns for a date range -- "'M' is deprecated and will be removed in a future version, please use 'ME' instead." -- and in the same branch of the same function, twenty-two lines further down, raises for a period range, "for Period, please use 'M' instead of 'ME'". A schedule written with one spelling warns and a schedule written with the other raises, and no single spelling is accepted by both calls, though the two calls agree on every date they produce: the deprecated month-end offset walks exactly the ends of the periods the period range names.

The oldest guard module to be examined this way is handoff_guards_v15, whose case a_bar_takes_a_width_not_an_end_date types the day number 20706.0, the two drawn widths and the header row a workbook came back with. Its primitives are matplotlib 3.11.1's date2num, num2date and Axes.broken_barh, and XlsxWriter 3.2.9's Worksheet.add_table, each read at its pinned tag rather than recalled. date2num returns "Number of days since the epoch" and num2date returns datetime objects "returned in timezone *tz*", both in raw.githubusercontent.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/v3.11.1/lib/matplotlib/dates.py; broken_barh takes a "sequence of tuples (*xmin*, *xwidth*)" and for each one "a rectangle is drawn from *xmin* to *xmin* + *xwidth*", in .../v3.11.1/lib/matplotlib/axes/_axes.py; add_table is documented at raw.githubusercontent.com/jmcnamara/XlsxWriter/RELEASE_3.2.9/xlsxwriter/worksheet.py as returning 0 for success and -1, -2 or -3 for the three ways it can fail, and the same file gives every column of a table the default name "Column" + str(col_id) and writes it into the sheet under the comment "Write the column headers to the worksheet." unless the call declared a header for that column. Rule 2a's search for the chart half found two independent numberings of a calendar date and no independent implementation of a rectangle's extents, which is not a gap: the width of a bar is checked against the length of the interval that was generated, an invariant of the input rather than a value anyone typed. The two numberings are CPython's own date.toordinal, which counts from a different origin and is not matplotlib's code, and Ruby 3.3.6's Date#jd, a C implementation in another runtime documented in ext/date/date_core.c at tag v3_3_6 as returning the Julian day number. Over generated dates the offset between matplotlib's numbering and the ordinal is one constant, the gaps between consecutive dates are identical in both, and the number of days between the two ends of a bar is the same in matplotlib's numbering and in Ruby's. For the workbook half the second implementations are readers, because the claim is about what one writer leaves in the file: openpyxl 3.1.5 and the Rust calamine reader through python-calamine 0.8.2 return the same grid for every generated schedule. The typed 20706.0 was the whole finding and it survives, enlarged. Handed the generated interval's length where the width belongs, broken_barh draws a bar exactly that many days wide; handed the finish date's day number instead -- the same two values, passed the way a reader of the call might expect -- it draws a bar as wide as the entire span from the epoch and reports nothing. Two further things the case did not say. A finish that precedes its start is refused by the guard module's own code and not by matplotlib: handed the reversed pair, broken_barh returns a rectangle with the same two edges and the same width as the correct one, so the two are the same bar on the page and no chart can show the error. And the round trip through the numbering does not return what went into it: num2date gives midnight of that day in a configured zone, which equals the date only after .date() is taken, and comparing it with the naive datetime of the same day raises TypeError instead of answering. The workbook finding is that one option decides whether a schedule can be read back at all. With the columns declared, both readers return the generated column names and the generated body. Without them, the header row the workbook already held is gone, and what replaces it does not depend on it: two schedules whose column names differ come back with the same first row, in both readers, so this is in the file rather than in one reader. Nothing in the file records which call was used. The refusal path is worse than the case recorded, too. add_table reports a range that runs off the end of the sheet by returning a code, so a caller that does not read the return value is told nothing, and reports a range overlapping a table already added by raising xlsxwriter.exceptions.OverlappingRange. One call has two failure channels, and the guard module's own `if code != 0` sees only one of them.

The same module's case an_empty_day_list_becomes_a_phantom_day types the three exploded rows, the one null among them and two float sums. The primitive is pandas 2.2.3's DataFrame.explode, documented in pandas/core/frame.py at raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/v2.2.3/pandas/core/frame.py as "Transform each element of a list-like to a row, replicating index values", and the same docstring's own example shows a row whose value is the empty list coming back as NaN. Two independent implementations of the same reshaping answer differently. DuckDB 1.5.5's UNNEST returns no row at all for an assignment booked against no days, so the two row counts differ by exactly the number of such assignments, which is a count of the generated input and not a number anyone typed. polars 1.44.1 makes the difference an argument and documents both halves of it in py-polars/src/polars/dataframe/frame.py at tag py-1.44.1: empty_as_null is "Explode an empty list/array into a `null`" and keep_nulls is "Explode a `null` list/array into a `null`". With both on it returns the rows pandas returns; with both off it returns the rows DuckDB returns. So the disagreement between the two engines is one documented option, and a chain that counts rows after an explode has not said which side of it the count was taken on. Worse, the side is moving: called without the option, polars 1.44.1 raises a DeprecationWarning at the call site saying its default for empty_as_null changes in 2.0, and the two answers it is moving between are exactly the two engines' answers, so the row count depends on the version as well as the library. A second distinction pandas cannot express: an assignment booked against no days and an assignment with no booking at all are two different records, and explode returns a missing value for both, so isna cannot tell them apart afterwards and a chain that drops the nulls drops both; polars, asked with empty_as_null off and keep_nulls on, drops the first and keeps the second. What survives the drop is the same in all three engines, so the phantom rows are removable and the only question is whether anyone removed them. The effort split beside it is exact where the case says and inexact in a way the case understates. The daily share as a Fraction adds back to the declared effort for every generated pair, and the same share as a float is within numpy's default tolerance of it, so nothing looks wrong. Whether it adds back exactly is not a property anyone could state in advance, and the tests do not state it: the two regions are read off IEEE arithmetic itself at import, sorting every effort and day count below sixty by whether the float shares sum to the effort. Both regions are non-empty, the losing one is nearly three times the larger, and forty-one of the day counts appear on both sides, so the same schedule split over the same number of days conserves one effort and loses another. The zero case is the one the guard module blocks with its own check, and the primitives do not agree on it either: Fraction and the built-in float division both raise ZeroDivisionError, so the refusal is the library's, while numpy's float division returns inf and only warns, so the same quantity divided the same way becomes a number that passes every later comparison.

The third of that module's fresh cases, a_blank_matrix_cell_needs_an_explicit_state, types two filled cells, one blank one and the counts of each. The primitive is pandas 2.2.3's DataFrame.pivot, documented in pandas/core/frame.py at raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/v2.2.3/pandas/core/frame.py as "Return reshaped DataFrame organized by given index / column values." Two independent implementations reshape the same generated cells the same way: polars 1.44.1's pivot, read in py-polars/src/polars/dataframe/frame.py at tag py-1.44.1, and DuckDB 1.5.5's PIVOT statement, documented in the duckdb-web checkout at commit 6f6cd1659f0e2ddd1965b1d3f1833e7fc512e7ac (docs/current/sql/statements/pivot.md). All three hold exactly the pairs the cells named and nothing else, which is the first finding: a pivot carries the roles the data mentions, so a declared role that no cell names is not an empty column anywhere but absent, and the matrix cannot be asked about it at all. It appears only when the wide table is reindexed against the declared inventory, so the blank cell the case records is made by the declared list rather than found in the data. The count follows: reindexing the same cells against one more declared role adds one blank cell per task and changes nothing about the assignments, so a report of how much of a responsibility matrix is unassigned is a report about the list it was handed. The three engines do not agree on the shape of what they return. pandas and DuckDB sort the pivoted columns; polars keeps the order the roles first appeared in, and documents that as the default -- its sort_columns argument is "Sort the transposed columns by name. Default is by order of discovery." -- so on cells written with the roles in reverse order the two libraries return the same matrix with its columns in opposite orders, and a matrix read by position is a different matrix in each. Naming the columns, which is what the reindex does, is what makes them agree. The refusal is where they part company for real. Given the same task and role twice with two different codes, pandas raises ValueError('Index contains duplicate entries, cannot reshape'), raised in pandas/core/reshape/reshape.py at the same tag and shown in pivot's own docstring example; polars raises ComputeError, because its aggregate_function is documented at py-1.44.1 as "None: no aggregation takes place, will raise error if multiple values are in group."; and DuckDB answers. It has no choice about answering: its documentation says "The `USING` clause determines how to aggregate the values that are split into separate columns" and that if the clause is omitted "it defaults to `count(*)`", so a PIVOT always aggregates and choosing the aggregate is choosing what a duplicate means. Executed, the SQL engine returns one of the two codes for that cell, the same pairs as before, and no warning. Two of the three implementations treat a responsibility named twice as a malformed matrix; the third treats it as a question about which code to keep, and the chain that reshapes in SQL never learns that the question was asked.

The same module's case matplotlib_svg_needs_a_fixed_hashsalt asks whether a chart is reproducible, and types nine expectations about it: that saving the table twice gives two different files, that svg.hashsalt together with a suppressed date makes them one file, that the PNG is reproducible either way, that the shipped svg.fonttype is 'path', that the default SVG carries no text nodes, and that fonttype 'none' returns the six cell strings. The primitives are matplotlib 3.11.1's savefig to SVG and the two rcParams the case sets, read at the pinned tag rather than recalled. raw.githubusercontent.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/v3.11.1/lib/matplotlib/mpl-data/matplotlibrc ships "#svg.hashsalt: None      # If not None, use this string as hash salt instead of uuid4" and "#svg.fonttype: path" with the two choices spelled out beneath it, "path: Embed characters as paths" and "none: Assume fonts are installed on the machine where the SVG will be viewed."; .../v3.11.1/lib/matplotlib/backends/backend_svg.py holds the only reader of the salt, _make_id, which falls back to str(uuid.uuid4()) when the salt is None, and the docstring of _get_clippath_id, which scopes what the salt buys: it "allows plots that include custom clip paths to produce identical SVG output on each render, provided that the :rc:`svg.hashsalt` config setting and the ``SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`` build-time environment variable are set to fixed values." Executed on generated tables, the case's first claim reproduces and its remedy does not. Two saves of the same table differ, and the cause is the whole of it: the file carries a Dublin Core date that backend_svg.py takes from datetime.datetime.today().isoformat() when SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is unset, so it carries microseconds. Suppressing that date alone, with the shipped svg.hashsalt: None still in force, makes every generated table save to the same bytes twice; and two different salts produce the same file byte for byte, so the setting the proof fixes is inert for the figure the proof draws. It is inert because that figure has nothing to identify: the table is drawn on an axes with axis('off') and both XML parsers count no clipPath element in it, while a figure with a line drawn inside its axes has one. On that figure the salt is load-bearing and the picture inverts. The suppressed date is not enough, a fixed salt makes it reproducible, and two different salts make it two different files -- so where the salt matters at all, byte identity is a property of the string a reader happened to configure rather than of the chart, and two machines that each fix a salt of their own do not agree. The other remedy the docstring names is honoured: with SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH set the chart is reproducible without touching savefig's metadata at all, and the instant written into the file is the one pandas resolves that epoch to in UTC, which is a second implementation of the conversion and not matplotlib's line. This is the same environment variable the deterministic-package cluster above turns on, so one variable governs both the archive and the chart. The PNG claim holds as recorded, and holds without any setting: the raster carries no timestamp and no identifier, and saves to the same bytes twice with the date left alone. The font half is where the case understates what it found. Under the shipped default both parsers read zero text elements from the chart, so a reader searching it for one of its own cells finds nothing; what the file holds instead is one <use> element per character, in the order Table.draw draws the cells, which .../v3.11.1/lib/matplotlib/table.py fixes as "for key in sorted(self._cells)" with the column labels added at row 0 and the body below them. Each of those elements names a glyph identifier that TextToPath._get_glyph_repr in .../v3.11.1/lib/matplotlib/textpath.py builds as urllib.parse.quote(f"{font.postscript_name}-{glyph:x}") from a glyph index FreeType handed it through matplotlib.ft2font. Rule 2a's search for a second implementation of that mapping found two, and neither is FreeType. fontTools 4.64.0 reads the same DejaVuSans.ttf in pure Python: getGlyphOrder "Returns a list of glyph names ordered by their position in the font." and getBestCmap "Returns the 'best' Unicode cmap dictionary available in the font", both in Lib/fontTools/ttLib/ttFont.py at tag 4.64.0. It is named in matplotlib's own dependencies -- "fonttools >= 4.28.2" in .../v3.11.1/pyproject.toml -- which is worth saying plainly, though it is matplotlib that depends on fontTools and not the reverse, and the SVG identifiers come from ft2font rather than from it. The second is outside both: opentype.js 2.0.0 under node v22.22.2, an "OpenType font parser" whose package.json at tag 2.0.0 declares no runtime dependencies at all and whose charToGlyphIndex is documented in src/font.mjs at that tag as "Convert the given character to a single glyph index." Both agree with every index matplotlib wrote, for every generated character including the space, so the cells of the chart are in the default file as positions in one font's glyph table and are recoverable only by resolving them against that font. That agreement has a boundary, found by running it rather than by reasoning about it: on a cell holding f followed by i, matplotlib writes one <use> element and not two, and the glyph it names is exactly the index the same font's cmap gives the single character the Unicode database calls LATIN SMALL LIGATURE FI. Of the thirteen characters DejaVu Sans carries that unicodedata.decomposition breaks into two characters of the generated alphabet, three -- ff, fi and fl -- are substituted when the table is drawn and ten are not, including the st ligature the same font carries; which three is read off matplotlib at import and never typed. So the default file is not one glyph per character after all, and for those pairs a reader resolving it against the font is wrong about the length of the cell before it is wrong about its text. The other runtime cannot corroborate that one: asked to shape a string rather than to map a character, opentype.js 2.0.0 refuses this font outright with "substitutionType : 62 lookupType: 6 - substFormat: 2 is not yet supported", so the independent reading of the ligature is fontTools resolving the character the Unicode database names. Setting svg.fonttype to 'none' returns them: the text nodes are then exactly the generated column labels followed by the generated body cells, read identically by both parsers, and the file stays reproducible. The case's own remedy was therefore half right and half inert, and the reading it did not do -- that the shipped default writes a chart no one can search -- costs one setting to undo.

The same module's case every_code_decodes_to_its_recorded_url makes nine typed comparisons and one typed refusal about a QR code, three of them inside loops: that each of two URLs decodes back to itself, that the legacy detector reads the first and reads nothing from the second, that both codes are version 6, that rescaling the second through three scales does not rescue that detector, that a blank page decodes to the empty string, and two about the reference-card PDF that are left where they are. The writer is segno 1.6.6 and the readers are the two detectors in OpenCV 5.0.0, shipped here as opencv-python-headless 5.0.0.93; both were read at those versions rather than recalled. segno's make in raw.githubusercontent.com/heuer/segno/1.6.6/segno/__init__.py documents that "all parameters are optional and an optimal (minimal) (Micro) QR code with a maximal error correction level is generated" and that where no version is given "the minimal version which fits for the input data will be used", so nothing in the chain chooses the symbol; symbol_size there "Returns the symbol size (width x height) with the provided border and scaling factor" and error is the "Error correction level; either a string ("L", "M", "Q", "H")". OpenCV's two detectors have one line of documentation each in raw.githubusercontent.com/opencv/opencv/5.0.0/modules/objdetect/include/opencv2/objdetect.hpp -- "QR code detector." for QRCodeDetector and "QR code detector based on Aruco markers detection code." for QRCodeDetectorAruco -- and both inherit detectAndDecode from GraphicalCodeDetector, whose doc comment in the neighbouring graphical_code_detector.hpp is "Both detects and decodes graphical code" followed by three parameter lines and no return line at all. The one "will be empty if not found" in it is said of the output array of vertices, not of the string the chain reads, so the published documentation of these readers never says what an empty decode means. Rule 2a's search for a second implementation found four candidates and rejected three: pyzbar drives the ZBar C library through ctypes and no ZBar shared object exists in this environment, so it cannot run here; the PyPI package zxing shells out to a Java ZXing jar it downloads at run time; and qreader layers a detector model on pyzbar and inherits that dependency. The fourth was installed and used. zxing-cpp 3.1.1 is described in its own README at tag v3.1.1 as "an open-source, multi-format linear/matrix barcode image processing library implemented in C++", "Written in pure C++20 (public API is C++17 compatible), no third-party dependencies (for the library itself)", and its wrappers/python/pyproject.toml at that tag declares no runtime dependencies at all, so neither segno nor OpenCV is underneath it; since "version 3.0 the default writing backend is provided by the zint library", so it is a second writer as well as a second reader. Executed on generated payloads it reads back exactly what segno encoded, every time, and it reports the error correction level segno declared, so the level is a fact about the file rather than an argument nobody checked. The round trip the case never runs also holds: zint writes the symbol and the Aruco detector the chain calls reads the same payload out of it, with neither the encoder nor the decoder shared. The version claim is not about segno's choice, and the two encoders are not interchangeable either. For every URL in the family, and for every generated payload that stays inside one of the three QR encoding modes, the two draw a symbol of exactly the same number of modules, so that the case's two URLs come out the same size is a property of the format rather than evidence about either library. Outside a single mode they part, and hypothesis found where: at the payload 0000000& zint draws 21 modules to segno's 25. For a run of seven to eleven digits followed by one character outside the alphanumeric set -- segno's own ALPHANUMERIC_CHARS in segno/consts.py at 1.6.6, sitting beside mode indicators that file cites to "ISO/IEC 18004:2015(E) -- Table 2" -- zint splits the payload into a numeric segment and a byte segment and fits a symbol one version smaller, every time. segno's encoder says why: prepare_data in raw.githubusercontent.com/heuer/segno/1.6.6/segno/encoder.py is documented as "If `content` is a string, an integer, or bytes, the returned tuple will have a single item", so a string is one segment and segmenting is left to the caller. The direction never reverses -- over the whole generated payload region the smaller of the two symbols is always zint's -- so make's documented "optimal (minimal)" is optimal within the one segment it was handed, and a chain that prints a code for a numeric identifier with a suffix prints a bigger code than the format requires. What the case did find is worse than it recorded. Over a family of eighty-four URLs differing only in a month and a day, read off the detector at import rather than chosen, sixteen come back empty from cv2.QRCodeDetector at the scale the chain writes. Every one of the sixteen is read correctly by the Aruco detector in the same library and by zxing-cpp, so the codes are sound and the reading is not; and all eighty-four are the same version and the same symbol size, so nothing measurable about the symbol says which side a record falls on. The case's conclusion from rescaling, that "the payload is what decides", is drawn from the one URL for which it happens to be true: of the sixteen the detector misses at the scale the chain writes, fifteen are read correctly from the smaller image of the same code, and the sixteenth is the URL the case picked. For that region enlarging a code is what makes it unreadable, and both other readers read both sizes. The blank page closes it. segno accepts the empty string and writes a symbol for it that is not a blank page -- the two do not hold the same set of pixel values -- and both OpenCV detectors return the empty string for the symbol, for a blank page of any generated size, and for a valid code they failed to read, so that return value separates none of the three; zxing-cpp returns no barcode at all for either image, which at least does not name a payload. The guard module papers over exactly this with local code, raising its own Blocked from a wrapper when the decode comes back falsy, which is the rule 1 pattern of covering a library's silence with a hand-written check rather than recording it.

The same module's case embedded_chart_images_keep_every_pixel types six comparisons about two charts placed in a brief: that both fit on one page, that two images come back, that the list they come back in is not the list that was drawn, that it holds the same two images paired the other way round, that sorting by the drawn bounding box pairs each chart with its source, and that an unrecognised ordering is refused by the guard module's own exception. The writer is reportlab 5.0.1 and the reader is PyMuPDF 1.28.2. Both were read at those versions, reportlab awkwardly: its code is in Mercurial and the git mirror its own README names -- "A mirror only repository is available for git users at https://github.com/MrBitBucket/reportlab-mirror" -- carries no tag later than ReportLab_3_5_0, while www.reportlab.com is refused by the egress proxy here, so what was read is the sdist PyPI publishes for that exact version, src/reportlab/pdfgen/canvas.py and src/reportlab/lib/utils.py inside it. PyMuPDF was read in docs/page.rst and docs/document.rst at tag 1.28.2. Rule 2a's search needed nothing new: PDFium through pypdfium2 5.13.0 and pypdf 6.17.0 are both already in this file for the P163 cluster, and their dependency lists at those tags say they are independent of MuPDF -- pypdfium2's pyproject.toml declares no runtime dependencies at all, only build requirements and optional groups, and pypdf's declares typing_extensions below Python 3.11 and nothing else, with Pillow confined to an optional extra. The first claim holds and is stronger than the case put it: every generated image comes back out of the file pixel for pixel, from MuPDF and from PDFium alike, so the expected pixels are the generated input and no oracle is needed for losslessness. The second claim is the case's finding, and PyMuPDF documents it before the fact. get_page_images, which Page.get_images wraps, carries the note "In general, this is not the list of images that are **actually displayed**. This method only parses several PDF objects to collect references to embedded images. It does not analyse the page's contents, where all the actual image display commands are defined.", and get_image_info is documented on the facing page as returning information "for **exactly those** images, that are shown on the page". Executed, the separation is sharper than a mispairing. Drawing the same generated charts in the reverse order reverses PDFium's object list and leaves get_images identical, so that list carries no information about the page at all, and for one of any two orderings a chain pairing charts with captions by it is wrong. pypdf, walking the same resources in pure Python under the comment "# Iterate through all XObject resources", returns the same images in the same order, so the order is the file's and not one library's. What the order actually is comes from the writer: drawImage in reportlab 5.0.1 opens "# first, generate a unique name/signature for the image. If ANYTHING is different, even the mask, this should be different." and sets name = _digester(rawdata+mdata), an md5 hexdigest of the image's own RGB bytes, and the names MuPDF reports come back in exactly the order CPython's sorted puts them in. So which chart the referenced list calls first is decided by an md5 digest of its pixels, and changing one pixel of one chart can swap the pairing a chain makes from it. Two further readings the case did not take. A count from that list is not a count of the charts on the page: drawing every generated chart twice leaves as many entries in get_images as there are distinct charts and twice as many in get_image_info, whose MD5 hashcodes come back equal in the two halves -- documented as "Multiple occurrences of the same image are always reported. You can detect duplicates by comparing their `digest` values." -- while reportlab documents its half, that drawImage "creates 'external images' which are only stored once in the PDF file but can be drawn many times" and with an ImageReader "it tests whether the image content has changed before deciding whether to reuse it". And the case's own remedy is not the call it is built on. get_image_info reports the content stream: on a brief drawn from the foot of the page up, its list is still the order the charts were drawn, the same order PDFium reports, while sorting that list by the top of the bounding box -- which is what the case does to pair charts with sources -- returns them reversed. The remedy and the library agree only for a page whose drawing order runs down it, which is true of the writer the case used and of nothing in the format.

The same module's cases form_choices_match_the_declared_contract and readback_fits_the_progress_contract type the six field names of two actions, the three status choices, the initial value, the two fields that start blank and the readings of a filled form. The writer is reportlab 5.0.1's AcroForm and the readers are pypdf 6.17.0 and MuPDF through PyMuPDF 1.28.2, two implementations that share nothing: the first parses the object model in pure Python, the second reports the page as widgets whose choice_values docs/widget.rst at tag 1.28.2 calls a "Python sequence of strings defining the valid choices of list boxes and combo boxes" which "is mandatory and must contain at least two items". Over generated field names and generated option lists both readers return exactly what the writer was handed, for the names, the options and the initial value alike, so the case's first claim reproduces. Where the case is wrong is in calling that option list a contract. reportlab enforces it once, as it writes: _textfield in src/reportlab/pdfbase/acroform.py of the sdist published for 5.0.1 raises ValueError('%s value %r is not in option\nvalues %r\nor labels %r'), and it refuses every generated value outside the generated list. Nothing in the file carries that check afterwards. The same refused value, put into the same field through MuPDF's Widget.field_value and written back out, is returned by both readers beside an option list that still excludes it, and neither complains. The contract is one step further on, in the pydantic model the second case builds: created over the generated options with create_model, documented at v2.13.5 as a function that "dynamically creates a subclass of BaseModel", it accepts the value the form was written with and raises ValidationError for the value the file returned. Two halves of one chain therefore disagree about one file, and only the half that runs last says so, which matters because the case reads the status out of the PDF and into the model in a single breath and records the model's acceptance as evidence about the form. The reading neither case takes is what a field name means. PyMuPDF documents field_name as "A mandatory string defining the field's name. No checking for duplicates takes place.", and executed, two fields written under one name are two independent answers: setting the first through MuPDF leaves the second at the value it was written with, MuPDF reports both, and pypdf -- whose get_fields returns "A dictionary where each key is a field name, and each value is a `Field` object" -- keeps one entry for the pair and puts the second widget's value in it. So an answer recorded in the form is not necessarily the answer the read-back returns, and nothing on either side raises. The chain escapes that only because it names its fields after a running index; a checklist named after anything the action itself carries does not.

handoff_guards_v12.py's case the_month_grid_needs_a_declared_week_start types the first row of January 2024 twice, once for each of two week starts, along with the day list, the process default and the placement of one event. The primitive is CPython 3.11.15's calendar module, read in raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.11.15/Lib/calendar.py rather than recalled: monthdayscalendar is documented there as returning "a matrix representing a month's calendar. Each row represents a week; days outside this month are zero", and the file ends by building one module-level instance, c = TextCalendar(), and binding monthcalendar = c.monthdayscalendar and firstweekday = c.getfirstweekday to it, while setfirstweekday assigns c.firstweekday. Rule 2a's search for a second implementation found no Python one. python-calendar 1.0.1 depends on python-dateutil and computes a week as self.date.isocalendar()[1] in raw.githubusercontent.com/anthonykgross/python-calendar/master/python_calendar/__init__.py, an ISO week of the year with no first-day-of-week option, and calendarweek 0.6 offers ISO calendar weeks and Django helpers; neither performs the operation. Two implementations outside Python do. java.time.temporal.WeekFields under OpenJDK 21.0.10 was read in raw.githubusercontent.com/openjdk/jdk21u/jdk-21.0.10-ga/src/java.base/share/classes/java/time/temporal/WeekFields.java, where a week is defined by "The first day-of-week" and "The minimal number of days in the first week", dayOfWeek() numbers days "from 1 to 7 where the getFirstDayOfWeek() first day-of-week is assigned the value 1", and the ISO constant is declared "public static final WeekFields ISO = WeekFields.of(DayOfWeek.MONDAY, 4);". ICU 74.2's calendar, reached through PHP 8.4.19's intl extension, was read in raw.githubusercontent.com/unicode-org/icu/release-74-2/icu4c/source/i18n/unicode/calendar.h, where setFirstDayOfWeek "Sets what the first day of the week is; e.g., Sunday in US, Monday in France", setMinimalDaysInFirstWeek says to "call the method with value 1" if "the first week is defined as one that contains the first day of the first month of a year" and to "use value 7" if "it must be a full week", and the EDaysOfWeek enum sets SUNDAY = 1. Neither has any Python beneath it. With the minimum set to one day, both runtimes agree with the matrix completely, over generated months from 1900 to 2400 and every declared start: the same number of days, and every day in the same row. Java's relative dayOfWeek is also the matrix column. So the case's first claim reproduces, and so does its last, though as an invariant rather than a comparison -- the non-zero entries of the matrix are every day of the month once and in order, for any declared start, which is why the second Blocked in events_on_grid, the one raised when an event day is not in the grid, cannot fire: the check above it has already restricted the date to the rendered month. What the case does not say is that declaring the week start does not determine the grid, and three things it cannot declare move it. The first is a vocabulary difference: ICU's day of the week is absolute and starts at Sunday, so it equals the matrix column when the declared start is Sunday, and for the other six starts not one day of any generated month is given the same number by both. The second is a rule both oracles carry and the module has none of -- Java's factory documents that the minimum "defines how many days must be present in a month or year, starting from the first day-of-week, before the week is counted as the first week", and where the matrix's first row is shorter than the generated minimum both runtimes renumber the whole month and put the leading days in week zero, exactly as weekOfMonth() says: "If the first week starts after the start of the month then the period before is week zero (0)." The two oracles agree with each other to the day there, so the disagreement is not between them but between a grid that carries the rule and a matrix with no place to record it; no minimal-days concept appears anywhere in Lib/calendar.py, and WeekFields.ISO is inside that region for every month whose first Monday-week is shorter than four days. The third is the calendar system. ICU's Gregorian calendar reverts to the Julian calendar before a cutover its own header documents in icu4c/source/i18n/unicode/gregocal.h at release-74-2 -- "Default is 00:00:00 local time, October 15, 1582. Previous to this time and date will be Julian dates." -- so for every generated month of 1501 to 1581 it reports the same number of days in a different arrangement, while CPython's calendar and java.time, both proleptic Gregorian, place every day identically, row and column alike. Last, the process-global default the case names is worse than a default. Because monthcalendar is a bound method of that one module-level instance, setfirstweekday moves the answer for every caller in the process, and executed, the module function returns the matrix an object built with the set start returns and stops agreeing with an object built with any other; both oracles carry the start on the instance, so there is nothing a distant import could change under them. PHP's own manual page for setFirstDayOfWeek, in github.com/php/doc-en at reference/intl/intlcalendar/setfirstdayofweek.xml, says the setting "affects the behavior of fields that depend on the concept of week start and end such as IntlCalendar::FIELD_WEEK_OF_YEAR and IntlCalendar::FIELD_YEAR_WOY" and does not name FIELD_WEEK_OF_MONTH, which these tests show it also moves.

handoff_guards_v13.py's cases the_index_accounts_for_every_block and a_literal_query_must_be_quoted type eleven expectations about a search over three typed blocks: the row count, the two hits, the snippet, the two refusals, the three quoted queries, the escape itself and the shape of the rank. The primitive is SQLite 3.45.1's FTS5 extension through CPython's sqlite3 module, and because sqlite.org is refused by the egress proxy here it was read in the project's own source at tag version-3.45.1 instead, which is a better reading than the manual page would have been. Rule 2a's search for a second implementation found two candidates with no runtime dependencies at all -- whoosh3 3.50.0, a pure-Python engine, and tantivy 0.26.0, the official Python binding of the Rust engine of that name -- and the second was installed and used. Its pyproject.toml at tag 0.26.0 in quickwit-oss/tantivy-py declares nox under a dev extra and nothing else, and its Cargo.toml at that tag names the tantivy crate 0.26.0, chrono, serde and pyo3, with no SQLite anywhere, so nothing of FTS5 is beneath it. Three of the case's claims reproduce in that second engine and three do not. A bare AND, OR or NOT is a syntax error to both parsers over every generated corpus, and a quoted hyphenated term is read literally by both, returning the one block that holds it. The hyphen unquoted is where they part: FTS5's grammar in ext/fts5/fts5parse.y has the rule "colset(A) ::= MINUS STRING(X).", so a minus sign followed by a bareword is a column set, and what a reader gets is the message fts5_expr.c raises through "sqlite3Fts5ParseError(pParse, \"no such column: %s\", z)", while tantivy parses the same string without complaint and returns the block. The escape is worse than that. The doubled quote the chain produces for a phrase carrying a quote character is parsed by FTS5 and matches the block, and is a syntax error to tantivy, whose parser does not read a doubled quote as an escape at all; so literal_query does not make a query literal, it makes it literal to one engine, and hands another engine something it will not parse. What the case records about the rank is that it is a float. Two things about it are worth more. The last line of fts5Bm25Function in ext/fts5/fts5_aux.c is "sqlite3_result_double(pCtx, -1.0 * score);", so every FTS5 rank is negative and the case's ORDER BY bm25(docs) ascending is best-first, while every tantivy score is positive and its searcher returns best first; executed over corpora holding one term in documents of distinct lengths, the two engines put the blocks in the same order, so the ranking agrees and only the sign convention differs, which is exactly what makes that ORDER BY correct here and backwards against any engine that scores upward. The second is that the rank the case records is not the rank the engine computed. The same file explains its own floor -- "The problem with this is that if (N < 2*nHit), the IDF is negative. Which is undesirable. So the mimimum allowable IDF is (1e-6) - roughly the same as a term that appears in just over half of set of 5,000,000 documents" -- above the line "if( idf<=0.0 ) idf = 1e-6;", so for a term in every document of a small corpus the ranks come back around a millionth apart, and round(r[3], 6), which is how the case records them, merges hits the engine had separated. tantivy's idf in src/query/bm25.rs at tag 0.26.0 is "(1.0 + x).ln()" with no floor at all, and its scores survive the same rounding intact, so the collapse is in the recording rather than the ranking. Last, the snippet. The text between the two markers FTS5 was handed is exactly the generated phrase, so the case's claim that the snippet marks the matched span holds and needs nothing typed to check it; tantivy highlights the same match one bold run per term instead, so the matched span is not one thing across engines, and a reader shown a highlighted result learns which phrase matched from one and which words matched from the other.

handoff_guards_v12.py's case show_pdf_page_does_not_preserve_aspect makes four typed comparisons and one typed requirement about slides placed on a handout -- the page count, the equality of the source and target ratios, written once and run for each of three slides, the slide order, the blank note area, and the requirement that carries the claim about stretching -- and the ones about the placement compare numbers the chain computed before the call rather than anything on the page. The primitive is PyMuPDF 1.28.2's Page.show_pdf_page, whose signature is documented in docs/page.rst at tag 1.28.2 as "show_pdf_page(rect, docsrc, pno=0, keep_proportion=True, overlay=True, oc=0, rotate=0, clip=None)" with the parameter line "keep_proportion: whether to maintain the width-height-ratio (default). If false, all 4 corners are always positioned on the border of the target rectangle -- whatever the rotation value. In general, this will deliver distorted and /or non-rectangular images." The chain passes that argument in neither of its two branches. Rule 2a needed no new install: PDFium through pypdfium2 5.13.0, which declares no runtime dependencies at all, is already in this file from the P163 cluster and rasterises the same handout with no MuPDF beneath it, and over generated placements the two renderers put the ink within one pixel of each other, so the measurement below is not one library's artefact. What the measurement shows is that the case's first claim is false of the page. Its unfitted branch is asserted by comparing the ratio of the rectangle it asked for with the ratio of the source page, and by that comparison the placement is stretched; measured on the page, over generated landscape slides placed in generated portrait rectangles, the drawing has the slide's ratio and not the rectangle's, every time, and the case's own threshold of a tenth would have caught the difference had it looked at the drawing. The stretch it describes is a real behaviour of the library, reached by the argument the chain never passes: with keep_proportion=False the ink fills the rectangle and takes its ratio instead, and the divergence from the slide's ratio is then asserted the same way. That settles what the chain's own fitted_rect is worth. Shown in two independently generated rectangles with the argument left alone, one slide is drawn at its own ratio in both, so no rectangle handed to that call changes the proportions the slide appears at, and a rectangle computed to carry the source ratio cannot change them either: the fitted and unfitted branches of the handout differ in the pair of numbers the case rounds and compares, and not in the shape of the slide on the page. The hand-written fitting is therefore not merely a rule 1 violation for reimplementing what a documented default already does; what these tests establish is that it cannot alter the one thing the case measures the placement by.

P110 composes checked PDFs into a navigable review binder with pymupdf.Document.insert_pdf, set_toc and get_toc, and records "bookmarks_checked": 42 among the checks it shows; case 110 of handoff_guards_v11, binder_bookmarks_point_at_real_pages, types the page count, the section count and the whole table of contents as a nested list, requires that every entry's page number be at most the binder's page count and calls that "every bookmark points inside the binder", and closes by asserting that a zero-page document raises. The primitive is PyMuPDF 1.28.2, read at that tag in docs/document.rst (raw.githubusercontent.com/pymupdf/PyMuPDF/1.28.2/docs/document.rst), which documents each get_toc entry as "*[lvl, title, page, dest]*" whose page is the "1-based source page number (*int*). `-1` if no destination or outside document", and each set_toc item as "[lvl, title, page [, dest]]" in which "**lvl** is the hierarchy level (int > 0) of the item, which **must be 1** for the first item and at most 1 larger than the previous one" and "**page** (int) is the target page number **(attention: 1-based)**. Must be in valid range if positive. Set it to -1 if there is no target, or the target is external." Rule 2a's search needed no install and no new candidate: two readers of the same outline that share no code with MuPDF are already in this file from the P163 cluster, and their dependency lists at their pinned tags settle their independence -- pypdf 6.17.0 is a pure-Python parser of the PDF object model declaring only typing_extensions below Python 3.11 (raw.githubusercontent.com/py-pdf/pypdf/6.17.0/pyproject.toml), and pypdfium2 5.13.0 binds libpdfium and declares no runtime dependency at all. Both were read at their own tags for this operation, pypdf's outline property and get_destination_page_number in pypdf/_doc_common.py at 6.17.0, where the outline is "a collection of 'outline items' which are also known as 'bookmarks'" and the page number is "The page number or None if page is not found", and pypdfium2's PdfDocument.get_toc, PdfBookmark and PdfDest in src/pypdfium2/_helpers/document.py at 5.13.0, where get_toc iterates "through the bookmarks in the document's table of contents (TOC)", a bookmark's level is "The bookmark's nesting level in the TOC tree (zero-based)" and a destination's index is the "Zero-based index of the page the dest points to, or None on failure", returned by `return val if val >= 0 else None` over PDFium's own negative sentinel. Over generated section titles written one to a page, the three readers agree completely: the same titles in the same order, the same nesting for a two-level outline with MuPDF counting levels from one and PDFium from zero, and the same destinations -- established not by reconciling three numbering conventions but by reading the text of the page each reader's destination resolves to, which is the generated title itself. The case's typed contents list therefore reproduces, and it is a property of the file rather than of one library. The requirement built on top of it does not survive, and three executions were needed to see why. First, set_toc's documented range rule is enforced by a loop that never reaches the last row: the check at 1.28.2 reads `for i in list(range(toclen - 1)):` and then tests `toc[i]`, so an outline's final entry is the one entry whose page number is never validated, and a one-entry outline -- the shape of a one-section binder -- has no page number validated at all. Second, the value that escapes is not preserved either: a generated page number past the end of the binder is written out pointing at the last page, which all three readers resolve to the page carrying the last generated section, and a generated value below -1 is written out as the no-destination sentinel, about which the two index readers agree entry for entry. Third, MuPDF reports an unresolvable destination as the -1 its own documentation names, and -1 is below one. Put together, the requirement that entry[2] <= out['pages'] cannot fail on a freshly written outline: every row it could have caught was refused by set_toc before the requirement ran, the one row that escapes that refusal was repaired into range before the requirement ran, and the only entry that genuinely points at nothing satisfies the requirement more comfortably than the entries that point at real pages. That last entry is reachable in the ordinary way, by deleting a page from a binder after its outline is written, and the bookmark stays behind with -1 in it; the three readers all see it, pypdf and PDFium reporting the same list of destinations for the edited binder including which single one has none, and the requirement does not. What P110's "bookmarks_checked": 42 counts is forty-two entries examined by a predicate that no outline PyMuPDF will write can violate. The other documented constraint is enforced everywhere, including in the row the page check misses: a first entry at any level above one is refused, and so is a level that jumps by more than one, in the last row as in the others. The closing assertion is a third finding of the same kind. "a zero-page document cannot even be serialized", the case's own comment, is one writer's policy and not the format's: pypdf writes a zero-page PDF carrying a generated title without complaint, MuPDF opens that file, hands the title back and refuses only when asked to write it out again, and PDFium will not open it at all, reporting through pypdfium2 as "Failed to load document (PDFium: Success)." Three libraries, three policies, and the guarantee the case reads off its exception belongs to the writer it happened to use.

P93 builds a complete resource matrix from recorded handover pairs with scipy.sparse.coo_matrix and coo_matrix.toarray and shows "286 stored edge weights and 1923 unrecorded cells checked across the complete resource matrix" and that the "presence mask preserves unrecorded cells separately from zero"; case 93 of handoff_guards_v10, sparse_matrix_sums_duplicates_silently, types seven expectations about it, the first two being that duplicate coordinates are summed rather than rejected and that "a presence mask built the same way becomes a count", and it builds the mask itself with a Python loop under the comment "a boolean mask cannot be built by summing". The primitive is scipy 1.17.1 and it was read at that tag in its own source: scipy/sparse/_coo.py (raw.githubusercontent.com/scipy/scipy/v1.17.1/scipy/sparse/_coo.py), whose COO notes say "By default when converting to CSR or CSC format, duplicate (i,j) entries will be summed together. This facilitates efficient construction of finite element matrices and the like." and "Duplicate coordinates are maintained until implicitly or explicitly summed", whose canonical format is "Entries and coordinates sorted by row, then column" with "Data arrays MAY have explicit zeros", and whose sum_duplicates is "Eliminate duplicate entries by adding them together" and "an *in place* operation" implemented as an `np.lexsort` followed by `np.add.reduceat`; and scipy/sparse/sparsetools/coo.h at the same tag, where the dense conversion the chain actually calls is one pass in listed order, "for(npy_int64 n = 0; n < nnz; n++){ Bx[ (npy_intp)n_col * Ai[n] + Aj[n] ] += Ax[n]; }". Rule 2a's search found two independent accumulations of the same operation already installed and needed no new package: numpy 2.4.6's ufunc.at, read in numpy/_core/_add_newdocs.py at tag v2.4.6 as an "unbuffered in place operation on operand 'a' for elements specified by 'indices'" which for addition "is equivalent to ``a[indices] += b``, except that results are accumulated for elements that are indexed more than once", and DuckDB 1.5.5's GROUP BY with sum and fsum, read in the documentation source at raw.githubusercontent.com/duckdb/duckdb-web/main/docs/current/sql/functions/aggregates.md. numpy is not an independent implementation of scipy's summation in the dependency sense -- scipy is built on it -- and it is used here as the second reading of a scatter-add rather than as an outside oracle; DuckDB is the outside one, and it shares nothing with either. numpy's lexsort was read at v2.4.6 in numpy/_core/multiarray.py, "Perform an indirect stable sort using a sequence of keys." Over generated pairs whose weights are whole numbers small enough that every partial sum is exact, the three agree completely, cell for cell and total for total, so the duplicate summing the case types is a property of all of them. Outside that region the picture changes, and the first finding is inside scipy. It has two routes to the weight of a cell and they are two different summations: the dense one adds the entries in the order they were listed, and sum_duplicates reduces the sorted run with np.add.reduceat, which groups it differently. Over a generated scale and a generated weight far enough below it that one addition absorbs the weight exactly, the two routes return different numbers for the same three entries in either order, and which of them keeps the weight is decided by the listing order: with the cancelling pair listed first the dense route keeps the weight and the canonical route loses it, and with the same three entries listed the other way round they swap, exactly. Both regions are generated directly rather than filtered for. So the weight P93 records for a cell is a function of two things the proof does not state -- the order the pairs were listed in, and which of scipy's two summations was asked for the answer -- and the twenty-eight cells whose weights the chain reports are not determined by the recorded pairs alone. When the weight is listed between the two halves of the cancelling pair every IEEE accumulator loses it and they lose it together, both scipy routes, numpy's scatter-add, DuckDB's sum and DuckDB's own more accurate aggregate fsum, "the sum using a more accurate floating point summation (Kahan Sum)", whose compensation term is itself below the scale it would have to correct; only summing the same entries as fractions.Fraction returns the weight. DuckDB documents the general shape of this itself, marking sum(arg) as one of the functions whose "floating-point versions ... are affected by ordering". The second finding is the case's own remedy. Its comment that "a boolean mask cannot be built by summing" is false: at boolean dtype the duplicate summation scipy documents is a logical or, so the constructor the case already calls returns exactly the mask it writes a Python loop to build, and numpy's logical_or.at returns the same array over generated coordinates. The hand-written loop is a rule 1 violation with a primitive one dtype away, and the case's second typed expectation is true of the integer dtype it chose and false of scipy at the dtype a mask wants -- while DuckDB, which documents sum(arg) as one that "counts `true` values when `arg` is boolean", counts them at every dtype, so "summing the duplicates" names two different operations in the two libraries. Two further readings the case does not take, both from the library's own primitives. nnz means the number of stored entries before sum_duplicates and the number of distinct cells after it, matching a DuckDB count over a DISTINCT projection, so the count the case reaches by summing its hand-built mask is carried by the object; and a pair recorded with a zero weight, or two recorded weights that cancel, leaves a dense matrix indistinguishable from scipy's own empty one while the sparse object still stores the entry, until eliminate_zeros, "Remove zero entries from the array/matrix", removes it. So P93's separation of an unrecorded cell from a zero weight is real, but it lives in nnz and in the boolean matrix rather than in the dense array the chain hands on, and it survives sum_duplicates and not eliminate_zeros.

P81 authors a workbook with xlsxwriter, including write_formula, and then calculates and verifies it with formulas.ExcelModel, openpyxl.load_workbook and CalamineWorkbook; case 81 of handoff_guards_v9, formula_caches_must_be_computed_not_defaulted, types seven expectations about that workbook -- that a formula written without a value reads back as 0, "the default cache is a zero nobody computed", that one written with a value reads back as 2857, that the formula text is '=SUM(B2:B4)', that a missing source cell is None to openpyxl and '' to calamine, and that the computed total excludes it. The writer is XlsxWriter 3.2.9 and it was read at tag RELEASE_3.2.9 in xlsxwriter/worksheet.py (raw.githubusercontent.com/jmcnamara/XlsxWriter/RELEASE_3.2.9/xlsxwriter/worksheet.py), where write_formula carries the parameter line "value: An optional value for the formula. Default is 0." and write_blank is "Write a blank cell with formatting to a worksheet cell. The blank token is ignored and the format only is written to the cell." with an implementation that opens "# Don't write a blank cell unless it has a format." and returns 0 when cell_format is None. Rule 2a's search wanted a reader of .xlsx that is neither openpyxl nor calamine and does not wrap either. Apache POI 5.4.1 under OpenJDK 21.0.10 is that reader and its jars were already installed here for the P188 cluster, so nothing new was fetched; its dependency list at 5.4.1 is recorded in this file already and contains nothing from Python. It is reached through a new shim, excel_cell_oracle.java, which prints one line per cell of one column for each of the three values of POI's Row.MissingCellPolicy. The accessors it calls were read at tag REL_5_4_1 in poi/src/main/java/org/apache/poi/ss/usermodel/Row.java, where getCell(int) is documented "If you ask for a cell that is not defined....you get a null." beside the enum RETURN_NULL_AND_BLANK, RETURN_BLANK_AS_NULL, CREATE_NULL_AS_BLANK, and in Cell.java at the same tag, where getCellFormula returns "a formula for the cell, for example, <code>SUM(C4:E4)</code>". The first typed expectation reproduces and is stronger than the case puts it. The zero is not typed in the replacement tests: it is read off XlsxWriter's own signature, and openpyxl with data_only, the Rust calamine reader and POI all hand back that same number, so the default cache is not a gap one reader papers over but a total every reader of the file believes. The second expectation does not survive contact with a generated cache. When the cached number is generated independently of the column the formula sums, all three readers return the number the writer chose and none of them recomputes the sum, so "computed" in the case's vocabulary means only that a value was passed; a workbook whose cache contradicts its own cells is read back without complaint by every reader, and what P81's verification step establishes about a total is what its writer was told, unless formulas.ExcelModel is the thing doing the checking. The third expectation belongs to one reader rather than to the file. The f element read out of the sheet part with expat carries the expression with no leading equals sign, and so does POI; openpyxl is the reader that puts the sign back, so '=SUM(B2:B4)' is a property of openpyxl and not of the workbook. The fourth is the case's own finding and it reproduces exactly, openpyxl returning None where calamine returns the empty string, and the two columns are equal everywhere else. What the case cannot see is what that disagreement is about. XlsxWriter's write_blank with no format writes nothing at all: the sheet part it produces is byte for byte the part produced when the call is left out, so the workbook holds no blank cell for that row and no cell either, and the call the chain makes to mark a gap is a call that writes nothing. Written with a format the same gap does become a cell, and openpyxl and calamine return exactly the same column for both files -- neither can tell a cell that is blank from a cell that is absent. POI can, and it also refuses to settle the question: its cell types differ between the two files, and for one file its own three policies return two different answers, a null under the default and a cell of blank type under CREATE_NULL_AS_BLANK. So the reconciliation the case performs between two readers closes a question that the format leaves open and that a third reader keeps open on purpose, and P81's two-reader check is a comparison of two conventions rather than a check on the workbook.

### Architecture management / component dependency model  proven


## Requirements extension: public-data theoretical assessment

Study date: September 7, 2026. The extension starts at P191.

### Amendment 5: evidence status and append-only requirements

The original P1-P190 record is preserved byte for byte. Its last line ends mid-URL at `https://python`; no missing text is reconstructed. Its recorded executions, versions, numerical results, and fingerprints are historical claims of that record. They have not been rerun or recertified in this assessment.

P191 onward is a requirements and theoretical-assessment extension. Every full library chain is SPECIFIED_NOT_EXECUTED unless a later, separately identified execution amendment says otherwise. `expected` describes a test oracle, never an observed result. Public documentation establishes available operations and candidate data fields; it does not establish integration success or production performance. Any companion reference checks exercise only their named small model and installed functions. They never promote a whole proposed proof to executed.

The core execution contract remains: zero LLM reasoning intervention between functions or chains. LLM assistance is confined to upstream design of rules, adapters, and tests. Runtime semantics, routing, transformations, decisions, and presentation use versioned functions and explicit data. Source acquisition happens before an offline replay; remote resources must be archived and sealed before qualification. Signed human adjudications are explicit input events, not hidden interpretation between functions.

Public pages and dataset descriptions were inspected with web tools. Direct raw-file acquisition into this runtime was unsuccessful. Where local reference checks use public values, the companion input identifies them as a small manually transcribed web sample, with its source URL and record selector. A hash of that sample proves only its local bytes. It is not a hash of the publisher's complete dataset. No complete external event log or private banking case population was ingested.

### Shared acceptance contract for all added proofs

G01. Preserve distinct evidence dimensions: truth evidence {supported, refuted, both, neither}; applicability {applies, out_of_scope, unresolved}; execution {not_run, running, completed, failed}; authorization {allowed, denied, unresolved}; and solver result {sat, unsat, unknown, timeout}. A single Boolean must not collapse these dimensions.
G02. The controlled rule record contains rule_id, rule_version, source_id, source_selector, source_hash, original_span, normalized_span_map, actor, modality, action, object, condition_AST, exception_AST, scope, valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at, evidence_requirements, and authority_reference. Absent mandatory fields block promotion.
G03. An AST is an explicit syntax tree. A successful parse and a matching quotation do not establish semantic fidelity. Natural-language candidates require an approved mapping or a bounded, tested compiler whose supported language is declared. Unsupported forms remain unresolved.
G04. All handoffs carry schema_version, input and output identifiers, source versions, units, time-zone and interval conventions, assumptions, missing-value states, and stable record-level provenance. Native library objects must be converted through tested adapters. A common JSON envelope alone does not establish common semantics.
G05. Preconditions, effects, authorization, and evidence freshness are checked separately. A valid plan never supplies permission. A successful API response never supplies independent proof of the business outcome.
G06. Every negative test names the input mutation and expected rejection or unresolved state. Every differential test compares an independently specified oracle; two adapters derived from one erroneous compiler can agree and still be wrong.
G07. Each public-data test separates observed records, published schedules, normative specifications, publisher-generated synthetic examples, and assessment-authored fixtures. Cross-domain analogues establish mechanics only. Domain validity needs owner-approved policy, complete case data, role authority, and acceptance evidence.
G08. A source URL, sample row, test declaration, solver timeout, or missing row never creates a pass. Full-chain promotion needs archived source bytes, environment lock, implementation hashes, commands, fresh test output, negative tests, output readback, replay checks, and measured coverage.
G09. Pin the environment only after resolving and testing it. Library references below are capability references, not installed-version assertions. Keep legacy Kuzu and Experta behind replaceable adapters. Do not force all engines into one environment before compatibility tests.
G10. Seeds, tie-breaking, iteration order, solver budgets, input ordering, and asynchronous event ordering are explicit. Distinguish semantic repeatability from byte-identical output. External side effects require authorization, idempotency, reconciliation, and a durable audit record.
G11. Network/import audit hooks and static scanning are defense-in-depth checks, not a security sandbox. Qualified execution needs an external isolation and egress policy, including native code and subprocesses.
G12. Checkpoints contain the whole legacy file plus all additions through that batch. The authoritative local file retains its original name. New proof IDs are consecutive and unique. Checkpoint hashes live outside the files they hash, avoiding self-reference.

### Limits carried forward into the extension

A lemma match does not establish the same requirement. Discussion order does not establish execution order. A current roster does not establish historical voting eligibility. A structural check that cannot decide soundness must report undecided. A reversed step list is not a verified compensation procedure. Timing gaps do not establish task effort or a causal bottleneck. Existing source-backed presentation and arithmetic evidence remains useful within its original scope. These restrictions govern new requirements and do not rewrite old results.

The plan is a private design basis, not a public regulatory authority. No internal names, case data, or source text were submitted to public searches.
